articles.content_orig:
Oil prices rose on Thursday, reversing earlier losses, following a report that Chinese refiners have suspended October fuel exports, further squeezing war-constrained energy markets.
International benchmark Brent crude with December expiry was last seen trading 2.4% higher at $100.36 per barrel, having earlier traded 1% lower, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures with November expiry rose 2.5% to $92.70.
Reuters reported that China's state oil major PetroChina canceled a handful of gasoline and jet fuel shipments that were planned for October, citing multiple unnamed sources, as Beijing looks to safeguard domestic supplies. CNBC could not independently verify the report.
Global energy markets have been grappling with supply disruptions from the U.S.-Iran war in the Middle East and Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Oil prices had moved higher earlier in the session as investors parsed a recovery in Middle East crude exports.
UOB in a note Thursday said that crude flows from Middle East were reportedly nearing pre-war levels, but fuel supplies, particularly gasoline, were lagging behind.
Worries over crude supply disruptions have eased following the resumption of oil tanker ​loadings by Saudi Arabia from its Red Sea port of Yanbu after the kingdom restarted operations on its East-West Pipeline.
"The pipeline has done much of the heavy lifting when it came to moving crude out of the Gulf," given that Iran has blocked the Strait of Hormuz, said David Morrison, senior market analyst at Trade Nation on Wednesday.
"Analysts say that the pipeline is nowhere near running at full capacity. But the fact that it is open provides some relief and has helped oil prices retreat," Morrison added.
Traders continue to keep a close eye on developments in the Middle East amid concerns that a lasting resolution to the Iran conflict may be delayed, with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio ordering the Iranian delegation visiting America to leave as the UN General Assembly was over, according to MS Now.
U.S. and Iranian officials had reportedly held separate indirect talks with mediators on Monday, while in New York for the UNGA.

articles.title_zh: Tesla upgrades China Model 3 with 16-inch screen and V2L, US left out
articles.content_orig:
Tesla China is upgrading every Model 3 it sells with a larger 16-inch touchscreen and a new light gray interior option, and it’s turning on up to 2.2 kW of AC power export across its entire Model 3 and Model Y lineup in the country.
The US Model 3 gets none of it. Tesla’s American Model 3 still has a 15.4-inch display, and it’s shut out of the vehicle-to-load feature Tesla launched stateside in August.
Tesla announced the changes on October 1 with a set of four marketing posters on its official Chinese channels.
The main hardware change is the center display. Every current Model 3 trim in China now gets a 16-inch touchscreen, up from 15.4 inches. Tesla says it has a higher resolution and a higher refresh rate, but it didn’t give actual numbers for either.
The second change is cosmetic. Chinese buyers can now option a light gray “premium interior,” which Tesla pairs with a black fabric headliner. That’s the same move Tesla made on the US Model Y Premium back in January, when it added a black headliner and the 16-inch screen to the 2026 Model Y .
Then there’s power export. Every Model 3 and Model Y currently on sale in China can now push out up to 2,200 W of AC power. Tesla’s example is a camping setup running a 600 W rice cooker, a 1 kW hot pot, and a 600 W electric kettle at the same time.
Owners need to buy Tesla’s AC power-export adapter to use it. The only exception is the three-row Model Y L, which doesn’t need the adapter.
The upgrades came bundled with a new round of incentives. Model 3 orders placed by October 31 get 5,000 yuan (~$740) off the final payment.
Tesla is stacking that with 5-year 0% financing (79,900 yuan down, from about 2,377 yuan per month), an 8,000 yuan insurance subsidy on the RWD, Long Range RWD, and Long Range AWD, an 8,000 yuan paint credit, and a choice of three charging perks.
After all that, Tesla advertises the Model 3 from 222,500 yuan (~$33,000). But the list price didn’t move. The base RWD is still 235,500 yuan, so the headline price only works once you count both the final-payment discount and the insurance subsidy.
Even after discounts, it’s well above BYD’s new Formula S, which starts at 189,900 yuan for the RWD sedan .
We only at least try to pretend to compete where we feel the pressure of competition. The others can live with the scrubs.
We are not a car company, we are a company promising business models but having none.
The competition is fierce in China and Tesla is launching new features and incentives there first.
In the US, the Model 3 starts at $36,990, and Tesla’s own spec page still lists a 15.4-inch center touchscreen.
V2L is the bigger gap. When Tesla brought vehicle-to-load to the US in August , it limited it to the Model Y Premium, Model Y Performance, and Cybertruck, at 2.4 kW through an $80 adapter for the Gen 3 Mobile Connector. The entire US Model 3 lineup was left out. In China, every Model 3 gets it.

articles.title_orig: Japan Raises Residency Fees 2,000 Percent Amid ‘Anxiety’ Over Foreigners
articles.title_zh: Japan Raises Residency Fees 2,000 Percent Amid ‘Anxiety’ Over Foreigners
articles.content_orig:
The hikes are part of immigration policy changes introduced to manage Japan's growing foreign population
Japan has raised fees for foreigners seeking permanent residency in the country by 20 times to 200,000 yen ($1,270; Â£955).
Those seeking permanent residency must now also meet new income, pension and Japanese-language requirements.
Long lines formed outside immigration offices earlier this week as applicants sought to beat the fee hikes, with Tokyo's main immigration bureau reporting wait times of over seven hours.
The fee increases are part of a series of changes to Japan's immigration policy under Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, which aim to manage its rapidly growing foreign population.
In July, Japan implemented a five-fold increase in visa fees for all foreigners â its first visa fee hike in 50 years. Authorities said this was meant to "reflect inflation and exchange rate fluctuations".
Although immigration remains politically sensitive and restrictive in Japan, the nation's ageing population is increasingly relying on foreign workers to plug a labour shortage.
Japan's foreign resident population surpassed 4.12 million at the end of 2025, marking a record 9.5% increase from the previous year. This however has led to growing anxieties over immigration and social change.
Takaichi has made managing immigration one of her key priorities since she took office in October last year.
In an X post days before the residency permit hikes set in, Takaichi wrote that her government recognises that "some members of the public may feel a sense of concern or unfairness" as Japan's foreign resident population grows.
"To address these concerns, [the government] is working to ensure that its policies toward foreign nationals are orderly, and that both Japanese citizens and foreign residents can live safely and securely," she wrote.
Before the hikes, it would cost non-permanent residents in Japan 6,000 yen each time they applied to change their residency status or extend their period of stay.
From 1 October, the fee varies according to the duration of stay sought â from 10,000 yen for three months or less, to 75,000 yen for five years or more.
Applicants who face financial hardship or are designated as refugees would be granted discounts.
Aspiring permanent residents must now also earn a stable income at or above the Japanese average. Latest data released in July puts average household income at 5.75 million yen as of 2024.
Micaiah Stevens, who has been living and working in Tokyo for 10 years, was not able to compile the necessary documentation to submit his application for permanent residency before the price hike.
The 37-year-old still plans to apply, but questions the new measures aimed at foreign residents.
"My immediate reaction was that foreigners were being treated a bit too conveniently. We're being asked to make more than the average Japanese person, pay a significantly higher fee, just to be able to work in Japan and provide taxes," he tells the BBC.
"There's already a significant language and cultural barrier that prevents some talent from coming over. This just doesn't strike me as a plan that was thought out to the long term."
From April next year, permanent residency applicants will face even tighter requirements, including basic Japanese language proficiency. This has led to a surge in enrollments at Japanese language schools as well as people signing up to take the Japanese-Language Proficiency Test, local media reported.
Applicants' expected pension benefits must also be equivalent to that of someone who has enrolled into the employee pension system for 30 years, although the value of one's financial assets can be considered if their expected pension benefits fall short.

articles.title_orig: Red Sox vs. Yankees live updates, news, starting pitchers for Game 2: Sonny Gray, Max Fried take the mound Wednesday
articles.title_zh: Red Sox vs. Yankees live updates, news, starting pitchers for Game 2: Sonny Gray, Max Fried take the mound Wednesday
articles.content_orig:
The New York Yankees have advanced to the American League Division Series. Convincingly.
For the second straight game, the club made its rivalry with the Boston Red Sox look far from competitive, winning Game 2 of their wild-card series 9-2 to finish off a sweep. The Yankees will face another AL East foe, the Tampa Bay Rays , in the next round.
The Yankees did this without Aaron Judge , whose health still looms over the Bronx . Game 1 of the ALDS is scheduled for Saturday at 6:30 p.m. ET.
Wednesday's wild-card Game 2 started as a duel between starting pitchers Max Fried and Sonny Gray but turned into a rout gradually and then suddenly. First came a Luis García Jr. homer to break a scoreless tie in the fourth inning. Cody Bellinger doubled the New York lead in the fifth with an RBI single, right after the Red Sox opted to pull Gray.
Then came the sixth inning.
It began hopefully for the Red Sox, who scored their first run of the series on a Willson Contreras homer that might or might not have received some help from a fan . Either way, Contreras and Fried exchanged hard stares during a long home run trot. Game on, right? Right?
Boston's next lever to pull was bringing in ace Garrett Crochet for his first appearance since April, returning from shoulder inflammation and a lat strain. It was a nice story, one that was soon ruined by Crochet failing to get any of his four batters out. He exited with his team down by two runs, with the bases loaded and no outs.
The Red Sox brought in setup man Garrett Whitlock to try to keep the game competitive, but productive outs scored two more runs. Boston then intentionally walked Ben Rice to set up a faceoff between Whitlock and Bellinger.
Bellinger made that decision look foolish.
Everything that followed was merely procedural for a lopsided Yankees win.
The Red Sox made themselves a playoff team after a start so bad they fired manager Alex Cora, and they could do no wrong for one magical stretch in the middle of the season. However, there was once again a clear talent deficit against the Yankees, even without Judge.
This is the second straight year that Boston has ended its season in New York, though the Sox at least played a Game 3 last season. This time around, they were outscored 18-2. The Yankees' two starting pitchers, Fried and presumptive Cy Young winner Cam Schlittler , combined to throw 12 1/3 innings with 5 hits and 1 run allowed, with 16 strikeouts.
The Red Sox had injuries, of course, their most recent being Roman Anthony in Game 1 . And it's not like we can pretend they had the fully functional version of Crochet. Still, this result begs the question of what the plan is under chief baseball officer Craig Breslow , who has appeared to steer the club into the exact kind of tier MLB teams want to avoid in the long term.
Yankees fans haven't exactly been thrilled with their team's recent era, either, but they at least get to watch their team play this weekend, with the hope of benefiting from a chaotic American League field this season. New York gets two full days of rest before its series opener against the Rays, against whom they went 6-7 in the regular season.
Follow along with Yahoo Sports for live updates, highlights and more as the New York Yankees host the Boston Red Sox in Game 2 of the AL wild-card round on Wednesday.
This one is over. For a second straight game, the Yankees were all over the Red Sox, and now they will head to Florida to face another AL East foe, the Tampa Bay Rays.
Boston's season, which ranged from turbulent to thrilling, is over.
Aroldis Chapman strikes out the side in the bottom of the eighth inning. He remains a tough pitcher to face.
The Red Sox have one more inning to make up for a seven-run deficit, so they can force a Game 3, so they can fly to Florida and face the Rays on Saturday.
Austin Wells knocks in another run, and that will do it for Garrett Whitlock. Carry on.
Warren has no further trouble and the Yankees are two innings away from a date with the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS.
Nick Sogard gets a run back with a line drive homer to right field off Will Warren.
Spencer Jones strikes out to end the inning. All the Red Sox need to do now is octuple their runs scored this series to force extra innings.
Cody Bellinger, whose dad, Clay, threw out the first pitch today, blows this game wide open with a three-run homer. The Red Sox intentionally walked Ben Rice into an empty first base, and Bellinger just made that blow up in their face.
A sacrifice bunt ends up just foul for Ryan McMahon, who then delivers a swinging bunt to score on a fielder's choice. And now an intentional walk of Ben Rice for Whitlock to face Cody Bellinger.
Wells hits a sacrifice fly to left and Jazz Chisholm Jr. takes third. This inning has been a slow motion crash for Boston.
Crochet's first appearance in five months didn't go too well. The Yankees now have the bases loaded with no outs, so the Red Sox pull their returning ace for Garrett Whitlock. He'll face Austin Wells as the Yankees threaten to blow this game wide open.
Spencer Jones reached first on a dropped third strike (thanks to an overturned call), stole second, took third on a bad throw to second and scored on a George Lombard Jr. single. The Yankees pull a run out of basically nothing to go back up two runs.
Fried gets out of the inning and in comes Red Sox ace Garrett Crochet to pitch the seventh.
The last time Crochet pitched for Boston, Alex Cora was manager.
Max Fried was a strike away from making it six scoreless innings, but Willson Contreras clubs a high fastball to right field, and a fan catches it. Replay review finds no fan interference, and Boston has its first run of the series.
Contreras and Fried seemed to exchange a stare during a slow home run trot.

articles.title_orig: Steelers trade Joey Porter Jr. to the Cowboys
articles.title_zh: Steelers trade Joey Porter Jr. to the Cowboys
articles.content_orig:
Last year, once the Cowboys realized that linebacker Micah Parsons wasn’t going to play without a new contract, Dallas traded him.
This year, the Steelers apparently have realized that cornerback Joey Porter Jr. wouldn’t be playing without a new contract. And so they’re trading him.
Per multiple reports, the Steelers are sending Porter to the Cowboys.
The full terms have yet to emerge. The separate question will be whether the Cowboys will give Porter the contract he couldn’t get in Pittsburgh.
Dallas could decide to ride it out in 2026, with Porter making $3.924 million. Then, they could apply the franchise tag in 2027.
It’s hard to imagine the Cowboys tradining for a player who apparently doesn’t intend to play until he gets a new deal.
The common link between Porter, a second-round pick in 2023, and Parsons is that both are represented by David Mulugheta of Athletes First. Mulugheta also represents receiver George Pickens, who was traded by the Steelers to the Cowboys in May 2025.
The Cowboys haven’t given Pickens a new deal. For 2026, they tagged him. For receivers, the franchise tender is well below market value. It is for cornerbacks, too.
Much will be revealed in the coming hours. For now, the most important point is that the impasse between the Steelers and Porter has ended with Porter being sent to a new team.

articles.title_zh: Yankees send Red Sox home again, move on to face Rays in ALDS
articles.content_orig:
Playing nine innings while wondering why not-ready-for-prime-time Chad Tracy thought it was a good idea to yank his two best starting pitchers after 4⅔ innings each …
1. This lousy new wait ‘til next year that the Red Sox stuck us with Tuesday night? It feels an awful lot like last year’s season sayonara . Maybe even a little worse.
In last year’s wild-card round duel with the Yankees, at least the Sox won a game, with ace Garrett Crochet delivering a gem in Game 1 . The 2025 Yankees won the next two in the silly best-of-three format, with Cam Schlittler and friends shutting out the Sox in a suspense-free Game 3 .
This year? The Sox went down wheezing. Schlittler, the heavy favorite for the AL Cy Young award, rendered them hopeless in a 9-0 Game 1 win Tuesday. The Yankees ended the Red Sox’ season with a 9-2 pummeling Wednesday night , and you don’t need a calculator to tally up a run differential between these teams. (Yankees, plus-16.)
The better team probably won last year. This year? There is no doubt. The Red Sox were outmanaged, outclassed, and as usual since the start of September, outhit . It stinks to lose to the Yankees once, and it double-stinks to lose to them in back-to-back years.
2. But if we’re being honest with ourselves, there is justice with this outcome. Red Sox chief baseball officer Craig Breslow did not build a good enough offense; we suspected it pretty much since their magical, improbable 32-5 stretch from late June through early August curved back to reality.
And wouldn’t you know it, their bats snoozed through another abrupt postseason stay. Yes, the Red Sox were stung by injuries . But deep retrospection is not required to recognize that they never quite had enough offense.
3. We have all winter to deconstruct this most peculiar, uneven season, but this we can declare now. Breslow must get at least one high-end bat, and preferably two, presuming the possibility of a lockout doesn’t halt team-building long before the games begin.
Some marginal players had wonderful stretches for the Red Sox this season, but earth eventually called them back from the stratosphere.
For the last month, I’ve been wondering what this team would have looked like if Breslow had retained Alex Bregman (28 homers, .819 OPS for the Cubs) and signed Pete Alonso (an American League-leading 43 homers and 113 RBIs for the Orioles).
4. I don’t understand any reaction to Roman Anthony’s latest injury other than disappointment for him and deep concern that serious injuries are going to prevent him from becoming the superstar his talent suggests he can be.
Anthony was good for 3.3 wins above replacement in just 75 games upon coming up to the majors last June as a 21-year-old. An oblique injury — rotten to have as a hitter, as James Wood and Drake Baldwin, among others, discovered this season — ended his season abruptly.
Just more than six months ago, he proved he belonged on stage with the best players on the planet during the World Baseball Classic . Hard to believe that was this calendar year.
5. Not much has gone right since the WBC, to put it mildly, and the vast majority of that is not his fault. He started slowly, which happens. A complicated hand/finger injury cost him four months this season, and another ended his season Tuesday night.
Yet in 126 career regular-season games, he has an .803 OPS and 126 OPS+ at 22 years old. It stinks that a player of such obvious promise keeps suffering legitimate injuries.
6. Oh, and it’s borderline pathetic that a portion of the fan base — no doubt including a number of hot takers who think they should get a weekday gig at WEEI whenever the next lineup shakeup comes — have taken to calling Anthony soft or some other synonym.
It’s not as if he’s sitting out with a sprained hair follicle or something. This is an alarming, recurring injury that makes you wonder if his immense promise will be fulfilled.
7. Turns out that Garrett Crochet , who hadn’t pitched in a big league game since April 25 due to shoulder inflammation and then a lat strain, wasn’t quite ready to get back on a big-league mound, let alone under win-or-go-home circumstances.
Crochet allowed four earned runs without recording an out in the sixth inning, though he should have had one — he struck out Spencer Jones, but a wild strike three evaded Adley Rutschman and allowed Jones to reach first base. A tip of the cap to Crochet, however, for giving it a shot.
8. Payton Tolle and Sonny Gray each allowed a single run in 4⅔ innings during their starts. Those single runs each gave the Yankees a 1-0 lead that felt more like 5-0. They both did their jobs, and as noted above, their manager should have allowed them to do it a little longer. Tolle was the best thing about this season, wasn’t he?
9. The Red Sox have not played a postseason game at Fenway Park since a 9-1 loss to the Astros in Game 5 of the 2021 ALCS . The Red Sox lineup that night included Kyle Schwarber, Rafael Devers, Xander Bogaerts, and J.D. Martinez. Five years later, the Sox could have used those guys in the lineup in this series. Yep, even Martinez.

articles.title_orig: Becerra and Hilton clash over taxes, AI and immigration during the CNN California governor debate

articles.content_orig:
Democratic governor sharply critical of Donald Trump for not passing comprehensive federal AI regulations
Governor Gavin Newsom signed laws Wednesday aimed at protecting California workers from the threats of artificial intelligence , including potential job losses and workplace surveillance.
The laws ban employers from using the technology to predict a worker’s emotional state by using their biometric data, require employers to send written notices to workers if AI is responsible for mass layoffs and ban employers from relying on AI to decide to fire someone.
The Democratic governor also signed an executive order to require state agencies to continue to refer to the technology as “artificial intelligence” instead of the term “super intelligence” as Donald Trump recently ordered US diplomats to use.
“AI should expand opportunity – not come at the expense of workers and families,” Newsom said in a statement. “As this technology reshapes the workplace, California is putting people at the center.”
He sharply criticized Trump at an hour-long event with reporters Wednesday for not passing comprehensive federal AI regulations at a time when industry leaders are warning about the technology’s risks. Trump said Tuesday that top tech leaders signed a voluntary accord to “self-police” AI development.
The governor signed a law this month requiring operators of AI chatbots to perform risk assessments before rolling them out and an executive order requiring the state to consult with experts to further improve oversight over the industry.
“We have to do a lot more in the absence of federal leadership,” Newsom said, leaving the door open for the possibility of calling lawmakers back for a special session to further tackle the issue.
The news conference came on Newsom’s last day to sign or veto bills before he terms out in January. He started the event by signing a law creating a tax credit program aimed at helping local news organizations – including newspapers, digital outlets and TV stations – hire and retain journalists. Newsom criticized what he called Trump’s assault on a free press, pointing to the president’s barring of news organizations from the White House.
Newsom also spoke about the upcoming midterms, which will decide control of Congress. He involved himself early in that fight by leading Democrats last year in a redistricting battle to improve their chances of winning more House seats. He’s said repeatedly that the stakes are high if his party doesn’t succeed in November.
“There will not be a free and fair election in 2028 unless we take back the House of Representatives,” he said Wednesday.
Asked if he had set a deadline for himself to decide to run for president in 2028, Newsom hedged, saying: “That moment will arrive when it arrives.”
Former Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris, who, like Newsom, hails from the San Francisco Bay Area, has also said she’s considering running for the job in 2028. Newsom told CNN recently that he would not run for president if she entered the race. He said the two have not spoken since that interview aired.
Newsom weighed in on a proposal to temporarily raise taxes on billionaires that will be on the ballot in November, which he’s consistently opposed. He said he respects supporters of the measure, including Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, who are committed to addressing income inequality in the country.
“He’s spot on about the balance between the rich and the poor,” Newsom said. “On this issue, we fundamentally disagree.”
Newsom’s remarks came hours before a gubernatorial debate between Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton.
“You’re going to ask me, ‘Are you going to watch the debate?’” he said. “No.”

A long-awaited report Attorney General Andrea Campbell dropped Wednesday detailing the sexual abuse of nearly 1,000 children at the hands of Catholic clergy landed in the thick of an already thorny legislative debate unfolding on Beacon Hill.
The 203-page report detailed a state investigation that began in 2019 and found evidence that more than 270 priests had abused children across the Catholic Dioceses of Fall River, Springfield, and Worcester. In issuing the findings, Campbell called for swift legislative action, including to eliminate the statute of limitations for civil sex abuse cases.
“If we care about the report, the findings, and the survivors, it is our responsibility as leaders who hold the power … to pass legislation that would allow for them to truly get justice and accountability, and allow folks who have come forward the opportunity to seek accountability,” Campbell said.
The call came with a personal revelation: Campbell revealed for the first time publicly that she, too, is a survivor of childhood sexual abuse “at the hands of a relative.”
Campbell didn’t bring charges against any clergy members Wednesday, saying her office faced “significant barriers” from Massachusetts’s statute of limitations. But the Democrat wants to see lawmakers pass legislation that would eliminate them for civil sex abuse cases, as well as language to remove the $20,000 cap for damages a charitable organization can be forced to pay when it is found legally liable for injury.
She also wants new laws to create an indefinite “lookback period,” giving survivors whose abuse claims fall outside the current statute of limitations the ability to revive them.
Conveniently, some of those ideas are already sitting on the legislative bargaining table. But they’re not so conveniently tied up in what could end up being one of the messier negotiations playing out over a sweeping primary care bill.
Versions of the legislation Campbell is pushing ended up in the healthcare package the House passed, thanks to an amendment pushed by state Representative John Lawn , a Watertown Democrat who has publicly spoken about being a survivor of child sexual abuse . Lawn’s amendment would eliminate the statute of limits on civil cases and remove the charitable immunity cap, while creating a narrower, two-year window for survivors to revive expired abuse claims.
The amendment was tacked onto the bill with little public fanfare, but there were some immediate signs of potential contention in the House.
Lawn — the House chair of the Legislature’s Joint Committee on Health Care Financing — was conspicuously left off the six-member conference committee tasked with hammering out a compromise between House and Senate versions of the bill.
House Speaker Ron Mariano chalked up the apparent snub to concerns about other aspects of the bill — namely, ballooning healthcare costs — telling reporters last week that he tapped House budget chair Aaron Michlewitz to lead negotiations because “who better to handle the situation of the state budget and healthcare than the man who’s done it for eight years?”
While the Senate has advanced similar legislation in the past, a matching proposal didn’t end up in its version of the bill, raising the prospect that the provision Lawn championed could end up on the cutting room floor. A spokesperson for Senate President Karen Spilka didn’t address a question about whether she supports such legislation, saying only that the Ashland Democrat “supports survivors of child sexual assault and is grateful to the Attorney General for her investigation.”
Advocates who have been pushing lawmakers to pass Lawn’s amendment used the report as a chance to re-up their calls.
Lawmakers should pass the legislation “without delay, so that every survivor has a path to accountability, and no institution in Massachusetts ever again decides it can simply wait out the children it failed,” the Boston-based advocacy group Enough Abuse said in a statement Wednesday.
Lawn said he’s “hopeful” the legislation he’s backing will make it into the final version, but noted that he hasn’t heard from the conference committee.
What does he make of being left out of the closed-door-debate? “No comment,” he told the Globe’s Anjali Huynh and other reporters Wednesday.
You can find more of the Globe’s coverage of the AG’s report here , or read it for yourself .
Should the Legislature act? Give us your thoughts here .

The snub — if that’s what it was — didn’t exactly hurt Wu. She steamrolled her main rival, Josh Kraft , in the preliminary election, winning so decisively that he dropped out days later.
But if there’s any lingering animosity over the lack of an endorsement from the state’s top elected Democrat, Wu isn’t letting it show.
Wu threw her support behind Healey and Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll Thursday morning, saying she was “proud” to support the duo in their own reelection bid “and to continue our partnership to build a Boston and a Massachusetts that work for everyone.”
Healey’s response read almost like a parallel-endorsement of Wu, calling her a “fantastic partner” and champion for Boston in a striking change of tune from 2025 .

The two Democrats haven’t exactly been joined at the hip since they each ascended to their current roles. They’ve differed on policy and politics , and found themselves on opposite sides of local races as recently as ... the beginning of last month, when Healey backed two incumbent state senators whom Wu was working to oust.

When WBZ’s Jon Keller asked Wu in June about endorsing Healey, the mayor said she hadn’t been asked to get involved in the race, and offered a pretty candid assessment .

articles.title_orig: In photos: China's Xi hardens Taiwan warning as country celebrates week-long National Day holiday
articles.title_zh: In photos: China's Xi hardens Taiwan warning as country celebrates week-long National Day holiday
articles.content_orig:
China began its seven-day National Day holiday on Thursday after President Xi Jinping used his annual opening speech to sharpen Beijing's message on Taiwan.
Speaking at the Great Hall of the People on Wednesday, on the eve of the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic of China, Xi said Beijing must " resolutely crack down on 'Taiwan independence' separatist forces, oppose interference from external forces" and "advance the great cause of national reunification."
The language is harder than in Xi's speech last year, when he said Beijing "firmly opposes" independence activities .
The shift comes days after Xi's state visit to Washington, where he urged President Donald Trump to outright "oppose" Taiwan independence, and to limit Washington's support for the self-ruled island that Beijing claims its own. That wording would be stronger than the longstanding U.S. position of not supporting Taiwan independence.
"It has been speculated for more than a year that Xi would do this, but it was the first time we saw him do it," said Allan von Mehren, China economist at Danske Bank.
The Trump administration paused a $14 billion Taiwan arms package in May and has struck a less supportive tone toward the island over the past year.
State leaders, including Xi, presented flower baskets at the Monument to the People's Heroes in Tiananmen Square on Wednesday, the country's Martyrs' Day, a day before National Day. Xi walked around the monument in tribute to fallen national heroes, according to photos published by state media .
Crowds in Beijing gathered on Thursday morning to watch the People's Liberation Army honor guard escort the national flag to Tian'anmen Square, with a military band playing the national anthem and thousands of doves released into the sky.
Travelers and city workers are heading out for the holiday, which runs from Thursday through next Wednesday. Workers often stretch the break to 13 days, by taking leave from Monday to Wednesday, spanning the Mid-Autumn Festival on Friday.
China's Ministry of Transport projects about 2.13 billion trips over the holiday week, or roughly 300 million a day.
Daily border crossings are forecast to average about 2.16 million. Bookings for domestic flights over 2,000 kilometers are up about 14%, and international ticket bookings are up 22.5% from a year earlier, according to official figures .
Golden Week is typically a gauge of domestic consumption, but years of subdued consumer demand mean heavy travel may not translate into bigger spending. Trip volumes and revenue rose during last year's holiday but remained around 3% lower than in 2019 before the pandemic, according to Goldman Sachs.
The authorities in Hong Kong expect 7.4 million passenger trips in and out of the city over the upcoming week, and Macau anticipates more than 5 million trips during the holiday.
At a celebration event in Hong Kong on Tuesday, Chief Executive John Lee said the city's first five-year plan would help it "share the rhythm of China's growth."

articles.title_orig: Why Lindsay Clancy’s lawyer is disputing whether she killed her children
articles.title_zh: Why Lindsay Clancy’s lawyer is disputing whether she killed her children
articles.content_orig:
The district attorney who’s charged Lindsay Clancy with murder for the death of her three children has not committed to retrying her.
A possible plea agreement has not been ruled out but Clancy’s attorney and the Plymouth County district attorney are tight-lipped about any possible progress on that front.
In the meantime, Clancy’s attorney Kevin Reddington, in a bid to avoid a second trial, has filed several motions since the case ended in a mistrial earlier this month.
In a hearing Tuesday, Reddington said at trial prosecutors did not prove Clancy killed her three children – Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and 8-month-old Callan in January 2023 – a statement that appeared to contradict statements he made while trying the case.
At trial, Reddington argued that Clancy was in a state of postpartum psychosis when she killed her children and should not be held criminally responsible for their deaths.
Lindsay Clancy holdout juror speaks out
After killing her children, prosecutors allege , she then tried to kill herself, slashing her neck and wrists then jumping from a window.
“Where is the evidence that she did this?” Reddington said while arguing a Rule 25 motion for a required finding of not guilty.
Clancy never actually admitted to the killings, but still there was not a full investigation into the deaths of the Clancy children, Reddington told the court Tuesday. “They just immediately assumed that this woman was guilty.”
When asked later outside court if he’s now asserting that Clancy did not kill her children, Reddington said his arguments weren’t new and he’s questioned the prosecution’s evidence in the case.
“It’s not new rocket science by any means. It’s the fact that they cannot prove probable cause.”
At trial, Reddington told the jury Clancy should not be held criminally responsible for killing her children.
“This was a woman that was suffering from psychosis at the time that she went down to that basement,” Reddington said in his opening statement. “She had no motive. She loved her children. She intended to kill herself. She didn’t fake that.”
Defense psychologist Paul Zeizel testified Clancy described a male voice instructing her to kill her children and then herself.
Massachusetts defense attorney Elyse Hershon told CNN, “Whether or not a lawyer concedes, though, that their client did it as part of the defense, the commonwealth still has to prove it was her.”
Reddington has argued that any trial for Clancy should be bifurcated – one trial to determine her guilt and then, if necessary, a second to determine whether she’s criminally responsible for the alleged murders.
The judge denied that motion earlier this year, which put Reddington in a position to determine strategically how to approach the question of Clancy’s guilt and the idea of her criminal responsibility, Hershon told CNN.
“Could he technically have said she didn’t do it, it’s reasonable doubt, and also, if you think she did it, she’s not criminally responsible. Technically, yes, he could have done that. But strategically, he made the decision to do what he’d have more credibility presenting to the jury, and he went with a stronger defense in his mind,” Hershon said.
Reddington renewed his arguments for a bifurcated trial in court Tuesday when asking the judge to enter a finding of not guilty for Clancy. After court he said if there is a second trial he’ll ask the judge to reconsider splitting it.
Lindsay Clancy’s status hearing concludes, with no retrial date set
A Rule 25 motion in Massachusetts is a defense request to the judge to enter a finding of not guilty because the prosecution’s evidence is legally insufficient for a juror to convict on.
Reddington went through elements of the commonwealth’s trial presentation, knocking evidence as circumstantial.
“When you consider the evidence that the government has, you have the exercise bands, you have the woefully deficient DNA, you have the woefully deficient fingerprinting, you have the horrific, ridiculous investigation,” he said.
Prosecutors’ case against Clancy is based on speculation, Clancy’s attorney said Tuesday. Reddington said any purported admission to killing her children is not admissible under state law because it was never corroborated.
“Where is the admission? Where does she say that she did this? And what’s most chilling is the fact that when she comes out of this obvious coma that she is in – Your Honor heard the testimony from the psychiatrist and from the doctors at Brigham and Women’s Hospital – She was told what happened. She had no memory of what happened,” Reddington said.
The prosecution’s timeline for the day of the killings in 2023 “does not match,” Reddington also said.
“Even the government, in their own closing, indicated to the jury that she did not have enough time to do this. The timeline is ridiculous.”
Prosecutor Shanan Buckingham said the commonwealth proved Clancy killed her children, calling Reddington’s argument “laughable.”
Surviving postpartum psychosis
A motion for a required finding of not guilty is standard in criminal trials, and they’re typically denied. The bar for granting one is high.
The judge views the trial evidence in a light most favorable to the prosecution, and the defense must show the court that prosecutors failed to present enough evidence for a reasonable juror to find the prosecution proved every element of the crime beyond a reasonable doubt.
“I would expect that the judge would let this case take its course,” Hershon told CNN, but also said Reddington’s legal arguments don’t come up in your average criminal case.
“We are observing a very high level of lawyering with Kevin Reddington,” Hershon said. “(He) has the experience to know and be creative about seeking remedies or seeking alternatives to being told no that you’re not taught in law school, and you only gain from experience. So, whether you agree with him and what he’s doing or not, it is a level of lawyering that is much more than you would normally see in a courtroom in the state.”
Judge William Sullivan took the arguments under advisement and will rule at a later time either in a written order or from the bench.
Sullivan said he wants to set a trial date at the next hearing, scheduled for November 2. He wanted to schedule the second trial at Tuesday’s hearing, but prosecutors and Reddington agreed it’s premature to set a trial date while several motions are still pending.
Sullivan said he’d hear arguments at the November hearing on issues related to a holdout juror and a defense motion to dismiss the case over double jeopardy.
If they do agree on a retrial date, Reddington said he’s not available for a trial before June because of his caseload.
Both Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz and Clancy’s defense team have declined to speak publicly about any ongoing plea negotiations.
Cruz said he hasn’t made a decision about whether to pursue a second trial.
“We’re working on it,” he told reporters after the hearing.
“We’re doing a very thorough review right now, and we’re going to continue to do our job to make sure that we do what’s best in the interest of justice and the interests of the three children,” Cruz said.
Reddington told reporters, “If there was a discussion of a plea, I wouldn’t say anything about it because it would be private between myself and Mr. Cruz.”
Reddington has publicly said he’s open to a plea agreement , but he wouldn’t confirm whether he’s been asked to meet with prosecutors to negotiate. As to whether a plea agreement is possible, Reddington said, “That’s up to Tim.”

Over the last few years, Chinese Android manufacturers have followed Vivo’s example of launching add-on “teleconverter” lenses for their flagship phones, enabling long-distance photography that the phones on their own could never match. Today, Huawei one-upped everybody with the add-on lens for its Mate 90 Pro Max flagship, which is not only a comically huge zoom lens, but also includes its own image sensor.
The 1-inch-type, 50-megapixel RYYB sensor inside the Ruiying Z10 is bigger than any inside the phone itself, so attaching this lens doesn’t just give you better glass, it’s actually a complete overhaul of the camera capabilities. And while other teleconverters have so far had fixed focal lengths, this is a true zoom lens that covers 24-240mm, with a variable aperture of f/2.0-f/4.5. This is almost a camera in its own right, only using the phone for power, processing, and software.
Impressively, Huawei also appears to have designed the lens to attach directly to compatible phones, instead of needing an intermediary case for a mounting point. The obvious downside to the Z10 is that it’s absolutely enormous, even by teleconverter standards — you’re not going to fit this thing in your pocket. But at 346g it’s still smaller and more portable than even most mirrorless cameras, and you’ll probably be able to take it into venues where cameras aren’t permitted, like concerts and sports matches.
Huawei says the Z10 is compatible with the collector’s edition of the Mate 90 Pro Max and its Mate 90 RS variant, the only two models in the new Mate 90 series with the screw-mount around the camera island. They have impressive cameras in their own right, with an f/1.4-f/4.0, 50-megapixel, variable aperture main camera using a 1.1.28-inch-type sensor; a 200-megapixel 4x periscope telephoto with the same size sensor; and a 40-megapixel ultrawide. The 6.9-inch OLED display can hit 12,000 nits of peak brightness, and it’s powered by a 6,800mAh battery and Huawei’s own Kirin 9050 Pro chip. articles.title_orig: Fed watchdog clears former chair Powell in renovation probe
articles.title_zh: Fed watchdog clears former chair Powell in renovation probe
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Reserve' s inspector general determined management and oversight failures contributed to major cost overruns in the central bank's headquarters renovation, but found no grounds for a criminal referral, it said in a report released Wednesday morning.
"At no point during our evaluation did we find reasonable grounds to believe that a violation of federal criminal law had occurred requiring a referral to the U.S. Attorney General in accordance with the Inspector General Act," the report from the Fed's inspector general states.
Despite that finding, President Donald Trump seized on the report to argue that former Fed Chair Jerome Powell should be "forced to resign" from the central bank's Board of Governors "at a minimum."
"He can't manage a Building, and he certainly shouldn't be allowed to manage his High Interest Rate Policy (only on 'TRUMP!')," the president said of Powell in a Truth Social post Wednesday afternoon.
Trump, while waging a sustained but unsuccessful pressure campaign to get the Fed to slash interest rates, has repeatedly accused Powell of mismanaging the renovation project and misleading Congress about it. His administration launched a criminal investigation into Powell related to those renovations, only dropping it as it became a major hurdle to the nomination of Trump's handpicked successor, Kevin Warsh .
Powell said in April he would stay on as a governor after his term as Fed chair ended "until this investigation is well and truly over, with transparency and finality." Powell can remain on the board through January 2028.
Trump said in the Truth Social post that he has asked Attorney General Todd Blanche to "study" the IG report "and make a determination" of what to do about the pricey construction project.
"This is Jerome Powell's fault, and he should be forced to resign, IMMEDIATELY!" Trump wrote. He added that if Powell refuses to step down, he should be sued by the federal government "for either corruption or incompetence, both of which are completely unacceptable."
Trump has continued to press for lower interest rates since Warsh's accession.
The IG's report cedes little to Powell's critics beyond his responsibility for management of the project as head of the organization. Instead it details a renovation project of the Washington facility that ballooned in cost by roughly a billion dollars from initial estimates as the Fed struggled with design changes and other issues.
The report finds the Fed estimated in 2020 that the project would cost $1.3 billion; as of August 2026, the board-approved budget has soared to $2.4 billion. Construction costs alone have risen by $960 million.
The Fed's board has attributed some of those costs to inflation. That was part of the problem, the IG found, but while overall producer price inflation rose 16% during the renovation, some costs on the project rose by far more. Plumbing and heating, ventilation and air conditioning costs rose by 223%, for instance.
The IG found that the Fed failed to enforce a guaranteed maximum price for the project, and designed a process that didn't result in rising costs being escalated to the attention of senior leadership. A bevy of committees was responsible for the building project.
Some critics have alleged Powell perjured himself in testifying to the Senate about the project in June 2025. The IG's office didn't specifically set out to assess that claim, but the report said the watchdog had reviewed materials related to Powell's testimony. The report makes no claims about any misconduct related to that testimony.
Trump sharply criticized Powell over the issue last year. That prompted months of speculation that the president might use it as a reason to fire Powell. The two men toured the construction site together in a tense visit captured on video in July 2025. Powell finished his term as chair on schedule after a judge blocked a federal criminal investigation into the renovations.
Trump has long argued the Fed ought to lower interest rates and said he would apply that litmus test to anyone he chose for chair. Powell said in January in an extraordinary video statement that a criminal investigation related to the renovation was a pretext to force him to lower interest rates.
The Fed's Board of Governors declined to comment on the report. The publication includes a letter by Warsh who welcomed the findings and said the Fed would take steps to adopt the report's recommendations.
The investigation was led by Fed Inspector General Michael Horowitz. He was appointed by Powell in June 2025. Powell requested the investigation a month later.
Congress designed the Fed to be independent from the rest of the executive branch. The agency is self-funded and manages its own budget.
Republican senators who were present for Powell's testimony last year have said they don't believe he committed a crime in his testimony.
"I was the one asking the questions," Sen. Tim Scott , R-S.C., said in an interview on Fox Business in February. Scott said he found Powell to be inept, but "I do not believe that he committed a crime during the hearing."
Scott said in a statement Wednesday that he welcomed the new report. "Inflation does not change the Fed's responsibility to manage its resources prudently and be accountable to Congress," he said.
The president has insisted that there was "criminality" involved in the renovation problem.
In December, U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro opened a criminal investigation into Powell and the Fed over the renovation issue. Chief Judge James E. Boasberg of the D.C. Circuit in March quashed subpoenas Pirro had issued to the Fed. The judge found there was evidence that the subpoenas were intended to "harass and pressure Powell" over interest rates, but no evidence of any wrongdoing on Powell's part.
Pirro in April agreed to drop the investigation to clear the way for  Warsh's confirmation.
But Pirro said at the time she was awaiting the inspector general's report and would consider reopening the matter.
"I will not hesitate to restart a criminal investigation should the facts warrant doing so," Pirro said.
Pirro's office said Wednesday that it was reviewing the report.
"Today's IG report reinforces the gross mismanagement that President Trump has repeatedly highlighted by the Federal Reserve's prior leadership," White House spokesman Kush Desai said via email. "Financial markets and hard-working Americans alike deserve a Federal Reserve with competence and accountability."
After the IG's report, Pirro and the Department of Justice "have no basis to restart the President's witch hunt against former Fed Chair Jerome Powell," Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., the ranking Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, said in a statement.
The report underscored the need for more transparency at the Fed, Warren said.
Warsh described the cost overruns as "outrageous" in an interview with Fox before being selected for the job. After his confirmation, at a press conference in June, Warsh said he was looking forward to reading the report and said his focus was on "what we can to be good stewards of taxpayer money."
In his letter with the report, Warsh said he plans to conduct a full audit of the renovation and that he has asked the General Services Administration, which oversees other federal-government building projects, to serve as the project executive going forward.
— CNBC's Kevin Breuninger contributed to this report.

The phone is launching now outside China, though Vivo didn’t tell me the price or specific markets ahead of time; I’ll update this article once I have them. An immigration judge has cleared the way for the leader of Wisconsin’s largest mosque, an outspoken advocate of Palestinian rights, to be deported on the grounds that he is a threat to national security.
Salah Sarsour was detained in Milwaukee in March by ICE officers . A federal judge ordered Sarsour’s release in June, saying he raised a “substantial” claim that the Trump administration was targeting him for speaking out against Israel and advocating for Palestinian rights.
Sarsour said in a statement on Wednesday that the immigration judge’s ruling was “deeply disappointing,” but that he intends to appeal.
“I will continue fighting to defend the right to free speech and to stay in the country I have called home for more than three decades,” Sarsour said.
The government says Sarsour's decades-old terrorism convictions in Israel make him a threat to national security in the U.S. and accuse him of lying about it on his green card application. Immigration Judge Jayme Salinardi agreed but tossed out the claim that Sarsour lied on his green card application.
Sarsour, who was born in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, was imprisoned in Israel in 1988 after confessing to throwing a Molotov cocktail and stones at Israeli military personnel. In 1995, he was convicted of attempting to hold weapons and ammunition. Sarsour denies committing those crimes. His attorneys say he was tortured and coerced into confessing in both instances.
Sarsour does not have a criminal record in the U.S., where he has lived since 1993. His attorneys say the U.S. government has known about Sarsour’s convictions in Israel since he arrived. He is president of the Islamic Society of Milwaukee.
Deportation to the West Bank, “means the end of my life,” Sarsour told The Associated Press in a Tuesday interview. One of his attorneys, Patrick Taurel, told the AP that Sarsour’s earlier treatment by Israeli authorities is “probably a good indicator of what awaits him” if he is deported.
At a status hearing Wednesday, Taurel pressed the judge to specify that Sarsour can only be deported to Israel and the Palestinian territories. Jordan, a country with which Sarsour has no connection, is listed as a possible destination on the deportation order.
Sarsour was instructed by immigration officers to list Jordan as his home country on an immigration form because his preferred entry — “Palestine” — is not a fully independent, unified state. But he “has no right to reside in Jordan,” attorney Patrick Taurel said.
“That issue is preserved on appeal,” he said.
Taurel said on Wednesday that Sarsour is being unfairly targeted.
“If Salah can be deported for his speech in support of Palestinian rights, anyone can face the same fate,” Taurel said.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio issued a rare memo in June 2025 saying Sarsour could be deported on the same grounds as Mahmoud Khalil and Mohsen Mahdawi, both advocates for Palestinian rights whom the Trump administration has tried to expel, according to court documents.
Before the judge’s ruling, Taurel said Sarsour would fight his removal and would likely need to demonstrate that he would face torture by Israel if he were deported.
“It’s a very high bar, although I think we can meet it in this case, given what Salah has already experienced, and given the government of Israel’s treatment of people similarly situated” to him,” Taurel said.
Appeals in Sarsour's case are due in 30 days. Salinardi did not schedule a future court date on Wednesday, and announced he is retiring and that Judge Craig Defoe will oversee the case going forward.
Jawad Boulos, who represented Sarsour when he was convicted in Israel, testified in August that Sarsour was coerced into confessing and that he wasn’t convicted of any charge tying him to a terrorist organization.
Boulos also testified that Sarsour was tortured while in the custody of the Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security agency. The Department of Homeland Security questioned Boulos about the torture allegations, questioning how he could know it was true.
Sarsour’s current defense team has asked why U.S. authorities waited until this year to detain him. Taurel said the government has known about Sarsour’s time behind bars in Israel for decades and that Sarsour never concealed that information from U.S. immigration authorities.
Experts on forced confessions and the treatment of Palestinian prisoners in Israeli prisons also testified in Sarsour’s defense. Israeli military courts have faced repeated scrutiny over allegations of limited due process and the high conviction rate of Palestinians. Israel rejects the claims.
In June, U.S. District Judge James Patrick Hanlon ordered Sarsour released from custody pending his immigration case. Hanlon found Sarsour could have a case arguing the U.S. government was retaliating in violation of his free speech rights and that attorneys for ICE and DHS had not explained why Sarsour was suddenly considered a threat after decades of legal residency.
The Trump administration has appealed Hanlon’s decision to release Sarsour from ICE detention.
Sarsour, who has Type 2 diabetes, lost more than 30 pounds (14 kilograms) while detained by ICE, and his blood sugar levels were checked only once a month, putting him at risk of organ failure or death, his attorneys said.
An investigation by KFF Health News and The Associated Press found that hundreds of detainees in at least 33 states have filed federal lawsuits with similar allegations of medical neglect.
Sarsour is among several people who have been arrested in the U.S. and threatened with deportation after speaking out in favor of Palestinians since the start of the Israel-Hamas war in October 2023.

articles.title_orig: MI5 warns UK universities over ‘theft of tech secrets by Chinese front company’
articles.title_zh: MI5 warns UK universities over ‘theft of tech secrets by Chinese front company’
articles.content_orig:
Security service says academics should stop working with and taking grants from firm backed by Chinese intelligence
MI5 China alert will send chill through UK’s cash-strapped universities
MI5 has issued a rare public warning to UK universities that China’s intelligence service is using a front company to pay for research by UK academics and steal the secrets of hi-tech projects.
Britain’s domestic security service said researchers and academics should cease work with the China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI), sometimes also known as the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT).
MI5 believes the body poses a “significant threat” and is now prepared to say publicly that the CGTRI is a front for Chinese intelligence, namely the Chinese ministry of state security (MSS). It said continued collaboration by UK academics could be prosecuted under the National Security Act 2023.
The Chinese organisation has funded 100 or more academics at a string of universities across the UK, in return for access to the research, which it is alleged found its way back to China’s intelligence service.
On Wednesday, the Chinese embassy in London issued a strongly worded rebuttal, describing the accusations as “imaginary and purely fabricated”. A spokesperson said: “We firmly oppose such baseless allegations and have lodged solemn representations with the UK side.
“Exchanges and collaboration between UK universities and China have always been conducted on a voluntary basis and in compliance with laws and regulations. Such exchanges and collaboration are mutually beneficial.”
The MI5 warning sent a shock wave through the UK university sector, with staff reviewing the implications for existing or future partnerships with China, and experts raising concerns about the rigour of the vetting process in sensitive research collaborations.
Areas of research targeted include AI, cybersecurity, covert communications and steganography – the embedding of secret data in seemingly innocuous files. MI5 believes it has clear evidence of sensitive information being passed back to Chinese intelligence, and the Guardian understands that some British-based academics were given honours and awards by the Chinese as well as research money.
Successive British governments have courted Chinese investment and encouraged academic cooperation. Sam Dunning, the director of the UK-China Transparency group, said: “It is reasonably obvious from the internet that CGTRI was focused on areas of high interest to the military and intelligence services.
“Granted, CGTRI used various aliases and have certainly obscured some funding streams, but as for the UK universities or academics who knew they were dealing with CGTRI, open-source research made clear that CGTRI had military or intelligence links.”
Vice-chancellors who spoke to the Guardian said they were not aware of receiving any funding from the Chinese institute, but warned that individual academics working on joint projects with other universities or third parties may not know the original sources of funding.
Prof Peter Mathieson, vice-chancellor of the University of Edinburgh and the lead for international security for Universities UK, which represents 142 institutions across the UK, said MI5’s warning meant that future collaborations with the CGTRI would be illegal.
“They are saying that anyone who has a link to this institute up until now has not committed any kind of offence, because it’s not previously been said this was a high-risk activity.
“Now that they have said it, we have to sit up and take notice. It’s very much a forward-looking directive.
He added: “I can’t speak for MI5, but I think what they are attempting to say is that people may not realise that the institute they are working with is connected to the security services of the Beijing government. And there’s no reason why anyone should have realised that, because it’s a new piece of information that MI5 has discovered.”
In the alert issued on Wednesday, the Security Service said: “MI5 has identified that the primary purpose of CGTRI is to fund academic research that directly improves MSS technical capability for espionage.”
It said that CGTRI had “very strong ties to the … MSS, China’s civilian intelligence and security service”.
The alert continued: “Many academic institutions and individuals will to date have engaged with CGTRI in good faith given CGTRI’s obfuscated links to MSS.
after newsletter promotion
“UK academic institutions are strongly advised to immediately review any ongoing or planned collaboration with CGTRI. This is to ensure MSS derives no further benefit from UK universities or research institutions. Further, academics are advised to establish the ultimate funding source when conducting any research collaboration with Chinese institutions, to ensure CGTRI is not involved.”
That MI5 has decided on a public alert as a deterrence strategy, rather than trying to pursue every single case, demonstrates the scale of Chinese state espionage targeting the UK. It hopes universities will heed the warning and immediately cease their work with CGTRI.
The Guardian understands that cutting-edge British research on scraping social media (gathering large amounts of information from social sites and apps) is among the data to which MI5 believes Chinese intelligence gained access.
The security minister, Dan Jarvis, demanded universities end ties to the CGTRI. He said: “This alert exposes attempts by Chinese intelligence to covertly benefit from the expertise and research of our academics, undermining our national security and that of our allies.
“I have written to all university vice-chancellors to ensure they support their staff to end all arrangements with this company, preventing further benefit to the Chinese intelligence services and ensuring compliance with the National Security Act.”
Responding to the MI5 alert, Vivienne Stern, the chief executive of Universities UK, said universities took their responsibilities around research security and national security extremely seriously.
“The sector has made significant investments in recent years to strengthen due diligence, risk assessment and research security processes, while continuing to support the international collaboration that is essential to world-leading research and innovation,” she said.
Chinese government filings suggest that CAGT is connected to the China General Technology Group, a major state-owned conglomerate administered directly by the government of China that is also known as Genertec .
The Genertec brand has a UK presence, with a company called Genertec (UK) Ltd, appearing to be owned by the Chinese state.
The British company, which has been registered in the UK for a decade and is based in a shared office address on Southwark Bridge Road, had £5.6m in the bank according to accounts to the end of 2024 – cash that seems to have come exclusively from a single property transaction.

Backpack has officially been crowned the chunky champion of Fat Bear Week after an intense competition with Bear 910.
Officials at Alaska ’s Katmai National Park and Preserve, where over a dozen brown bears competed to be named the heaviest, announced the winner Tuesday night.
“We have a new fat Bear Champ! Bear 89 nicknamed ‘Backpack,’” park officials wrote on Facebook.
Backpack won the finals with 103,334 votes compared to Bear 910’s 98,253 votes, according to explore.org , whose nature cameras captured the Fat Bear Week contestants.
“Your votes, your posts, your favorite bear campaigns, and your shared love for Katmai’s wild places turned this week into a collective story shaped by thousands of voices,” the park officials said. “It’s a reminder that just like America’s 250th anniversary, traditions endure because people keep them alive.”
The competition, currently in its 12th year, honors the resilience of the 2,200 brown bears living in the preserve along the Alaska Peninsula, which stretches from the southwest region of the state toward the Aleutian Islands.
Established in 2014, Fat Bear Week is an interactive initiative to educate the public about coastal brown bears, the close relatives of grizzlies.
Chunk — officially recognized as Bear 32 — won last year’s title at an estimated 1,200 pounds. He was knocked out during the first round of this year’s competition by Bucky, who later lost a direct faceoff to Backpack.
A total of 16 bears entered this year's single-elimination, bracket-style tournament to compete for the heavyweight crown.
"Fat bears are successful bears," explore.org explains on its website. The animals gorge on the abundant salmon that return to the Brooks River beginning in late June. It is along the river that they build up the vital fat reserves required to survive winter hibernation. To be included in the tournament, bears must frequently visit the river area.
In midsummer, adult male brown bears generally weigh between 600 and 900 pounds. By the time hibernation approaches, following months of feeding on migrating and spawning salmon, large males can weigh significantly more than 1,000 pounds.
Female brown bears are approximately one-third smaller. Bears may consume as many as 30 fish each day during this time of year, working relentlessly to eat a year’s worth of food in approximately six months.
During their winter hibernation, the bears go without eating or drinking and lose a third of their overall body weight.
Contenders in Fat Bear Week also included five bear families, reflecting the record number of families and cubs present at the river this summer.
A mother bear must feed and protect her young while consuming sufficient calories to sustain herself through hibernation. Cubs frequently face the danger of attacks by other bears because of territorial behavior or food scarcity.
Bear 132 and her three spring cubs successfully reached the semifinals, but ultimately lost to Bear 910.
Contestant profiles identify Bear 132 as one of the largest and most experienced mother bears at Brooks River. In mid-July, one of her cubs became separated from the family for several days and roamed the river corridor alone. They were reunited a short time later.

Resurfaced allegations of a gang rape at a Cornell University fraternity house have renewed outrage over what experts call a legal “ loophole ” in New York’s – and other states’ – sexual assault laws that can make it nearly impossible for survivors to seek justice if they voluntarily consumed alcohol or drugs before an assault.
At issue is the fact that the woman, identified only as Jane Doe, says she drank alcohol and accepted drugs the night she alleges she was sexually assaulted for hours and advertised as “free p*ssy” by someone in a Chi Phi fraternity member group chat.
The Tompkins County district attorney this week offered many words to describe Doe’s account of how the men assaulted her: disgusting, repugnant, offensive, morally reprehensible.
But he did not call it a crime.
“The young men who engaged in that conduct were morally wrong. It was disgusting, and so she reported that to the police, and the police investigated it. That does not mean – if it’s morally wrong or disgusting or offensive, all those things – it does not mean that the penal law was violated,” prosecutor Matthew Van Houten said on CNN’s “The Situation Room.”
His response has left many asking the same question: How could that be?
The answer, sexual assault survivors and their advocates say, is what’s come to be known as the voluntary intoxication “loophole” or “exclusion,” a gap in the law that exists in about 19 states in the US. It’s one reason countless assaults have gone unprosecuted, experts say, and adds to the overwhelming number of barriers survivors face in seeking justice.
Under New York law, a person is guilty of rape if they engage in sexual contact with another person who is “incapable of consent by reason of being mentally disabled or mentally incapacitated.”
Here’s the “ loophole :” A person is only considered “mentally incapacitated” under state law if they were temporarily unable to understand or control their actions due to the influence of a narcotic or intoxicating substance administered to them without their consent – or to any other act done to them without their consent.
Cornell University agrees to independent investigation into its handling of alleged sexual assault case
Jane Doe willingly drank alcohol before arriving at the fraternity house, where members led her upstairs, she stated in a recent state lawsuit. Then, after the men surrounded her and pressured her to take ketamine – a dissociative anesthetic the Drug Enforcement Administration notes has been used to facilitate sexual assault – some of them sexually assaulted her for hours, according to the lawsuit, which seeks damages against seven men who were allegedly involved.
Doe told police she was okay with an initial encounter but said she did not consent to sexual contact later in the night, according to a six-page statement obtained by CNN detailing comments Doe made to investigators in the weeks after the alleged assault. She also described being physically hit.
In addressing Doe’s lawsuit allegations, Van Houten this week referenced her voluntary drug use in his explanation of the decision not to bring criminal charges, which he said were considered when she first came forward shortly after the incident.
“The facts provided by Jane Doe’s statement do not allege that she was either rendered incapable of controlling her own conduct or that any drug was administered to her without her consent,” he said.
In New York and elsewhere, every legislative session presents a chance to amend the laws around sexual assault. The Cornell rape case has laid bare a systemic failure within the criminal justice system, said Stefan Turkheimer, vice president for public policy at RAINN, an anti-sexual violence organization.
Legislation to remove New York’s voluntary intoxication exclusion has been introduced annually for at least the past eight years without success. Some lawmakers have been pushing for change for even longer.
New York’s current law was originally written in the 1990s to address cases where people were “roofied,” or drugged without their knowledge, rendering them unable to consent, New York Assemblyman Jeffrey Dinowitz told CNN.
“Under the current law, somebody being voluntarily intoxicated, which happens all the time, is a virtual get-out-of-jail-free card for somebody who commits a sexual assault,” said Dinowitz, a Democrat. “And that’s just not right.”
In 2019, Dinowitz attempted to change that with legislation that prevents the use of a victim’s voluntary intoxication as a defense in sex crimes where the victim was incapacitated. He sponsored it again in 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026. Despite the consistent support of victims’ advocates and other lawmakers, the legislation has never made it to the House for a vote.
“To me, it’s kind of like there’s a binary choice here,” Dinowitz said. “Either you’re on the side of the survivors of sexual assault or you’re on the side of the people who commit the sexual assaults. And I know where I stand.”
Opponents have raised concerns that it’s difficult to nail down the exact point at which a person becomes too drunk to consent. Others have questioned whether a new law paving the way for more prosecutions would disproportionately impact people of color due to existing biases in the criminal justice system.
What Cornell’s Jane Doe told investigators in 2024 prompts fresh questions
The crime of sexual assault can make survivors feel incredibly alone, Turkheimer pointed out.
“The way to heal is to come forward, share with others, and find solace and protection and justice in that sharing – but that depends entirely on whether or not it is safe for that person to come forward,” he said.
“We really need to think about who we’re protecting and why,” he continued. “If we are actually trying to encourage survivors to come forward, we have to have people and systems who prioritize their safety.”
Changing these laws state by state has proven difficult – but not impossible. Last February, Summer Willis crawled to the Texas state capitol on bloody hands and knees to demand a change to the voluntary intoxication exclusion in state law that allowed her college sexual assault a decade earlier to go unprosecuted.
The lengths she went through to secure the win – that other advocates and lawmakers had repeatedly failed to achieve – paid off. The Summer Willis Act was signed into law later that year, changing the state’s sexual assault law and more clearly defining consent in Texas.
Willis made her way to New York last summer to throw her weight behind local advocates and survivors who were pushing to pass a similar law in that state. She told the story of her assault. They told theirs. But the bill was never called for a vote.
The legislative fix didn’t make it to a vote in 2026 either.
That was before Jane Doe’s story exploded onto the scene.
On Wednesday, New York State Assembly Speaker Carl Heastie, a Democrat – who had repeatedly blocked the bill from going to the floor for a full vote – announced he is forming a legislative working group to examine New York’s sexual assault laws, tasked with developing legislative recommendations for the 2027 session.
Turkheimer and others say it’s possible that Doe’s story has garnered enough attention to get the law changed.
Willis told CNN she saw herself in Doe’s account of sexual assault.
“The same law or lack of definition of consent which is prohibiting her from receiving justice happened to me over a decade ago, and happened to others decades and decades ago,” Willis told CNN. “Unless we do something about it now, then it’s going to keep on happening.”
She is now advocating for the passage of legislation in multiple states that will clearly define consent and open pathways for survivors to seek justice.
Willis has a message for the woman at the center of the Cornell rape investigation – and other survivors of sexual assault: “I believed I was alone for so long, and I just want them to know they’re not alone
