articles.title_zh: Hegseth confirms plan to cut 20% of US top military brass and rails at ‘beardos, weirdos and wimps’
articles.content_orig:
Amid latest extraordinary attack on diversity, US defense secretary also suggests military is retaining service personnel at ‘record’ rates
Send us your questions about how the Iran war will affect US voters in the midterms
The US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth , has confirmed plans to cut 20% of generals and admirals and declared “no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps” would be tolerated inside the country’s military.
Delivering his latest extraordinary attack on diversity, and dismissing reports of low morale within the US armed forces as “false claims”, Hegseth also suggested they were retaining service personnel at “record” rates.
The defense secretary pointed to those onboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, following concern over mental health and supply issues on the aircraft carrier, which was deployed for almost nine months. About “80% of the force” onboard was retained, he said.
Addressing lower-ranking troops at the Marine Corps Base on Wednesday, Hegseth boasted about the anti-diversity policies in the Pentagon pushed by Donald Trump’s administration.
“The only focus, as you know, in your formations should be training, readiness, accountability, discipline and lethality,” Hegseth said. “And when you pursue those things, you don’t have to walk on eggshells … the complainers, the ideologues and the poor performers are no longer in the driver’s seat.”
He added: “But it’s worth saying again, so the fake news understands it. We are no longer the woke department or the weak department. Simple translation of that: no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals. Just warriors.”
Generals “who clung to the woke department, or seemed to think civilian control of the military is simply a suggestion, well, they no longer work here”, Hegseth said.
Eight US navy personnel assigned to the Lincoln attempted suicide since the start of their lengthy deployment as part of the US war on Iran, it emerged last week .
Hegseth appeared to reference the carrier while attacking the media on Wednesday, insisting there are “disingenuous headlines about deployment lengths, patently false claims of low troop morale, or flat-out propaganda, as if it’s written by our adversaries”.
The crew of the Lincoln, which was at sea for 286 days, disembarked on 1 September in a Thai resort city. The crew had been scheduled to wrap their deployment in May, but it was extended amid Trump’s war on Iran.
During his speech in Quantico, Virginia, the defense secretary announced several new initiatives, including a a new Pentagon project which will see Elon Musk, Palmer Luckey – a top Trump donor and ally – and Newt Gingrich, the former US House speaker, work with the department to study the “future of warfare”.
The Guardian previously reported on how Luckey’s company, Anduril Inudstries, a major defense technology company, has received billions in government contracts over the last year.
Hegseth also took aim at Ivy League universities and liberal arts colleges during his speech – which Trump has targeted routinely since he returned to office. The defense secretary branded the institutions as “DEI-worshipping woke factories”. Notably, Hegseth is a graduate of Harvard and Princeton Universities – both members of the Ivy League.
Hegseth said the Pentagon would now partner with other institutions as part of its educational pipeline. Some of these schools, such as Liberty University and Hillsdale College, are known for conservative values.
Others joining the partnership are Louisiana State University, Mississippi University and Tuskegee University.

articles.title_orig: Opinion | How China became the world’s gold superpower
articles.title_zh: Opinion | How China became the world’s gold superpower
articles.content_orig:
Beijing built its dominance through innovation and meticulous planning, not superior natural reserves
Perhaps no story illustrates the secret of China’s industrial success better than its rise as the world’s gold superpower.
China has revered the metal for millennia, yet it has never had a gold-based economy. Its own deposits were simply too scarce.
In 1975, as China began its economic modernisation, it desperately needed gold to fund reform and build up foreign reserves. Despite its best efforts, it produced a meagre 13.8 metric tons a year. South Africa, then the undisputed king of gold, produced many times that. Canada, the United States and Australia each comfortably outproduced China as well.

articles.title_orig: CA couple accused of killing son-in-law at park charged with murder: New details on arrest revealed
articles.title_zh: CA couple accused of killing son-in-law at park charged with murder: New details on arrest revealed
articles.content_orig:
DUBLIN, Calif. -- A California couple has been charged with murder after authorities say they shot their son-in-law to death Saturday in a public park, days before he and the couple's daughter were set for a hearing in a bitter divorce case.
Shili Chen and Shouyong Zhang, both 77, were briefly in court Wednesday for an arraignment on the charges that was postponed until Thursday. Jennie Otis, a public defender representing Zhang, declined to comment. Chen told the judge through an interpreter that she didn’t have the money to hire an attorney. A public defender will be assigned to her case Thursday, Alameda County Superior Court Judge Diane Meier told her.
Jonathan McKinsey, a 40-year-old gaming engineer for The New York Times, was shot to death in the parking lot of a sports complex in Dublin, east of San Francisco. A police sergeant was driving nearby and saw him on the ground as witnesses began calling 911 and pointing out the couple in their vehicle, who were still near the scene, Dublin Police Services said in a news release.
RELATED: Dublin man allegedly killed by 77-year-old in-laws was New York Times engineering director
Police detained the couple as they were driving away in the parking lot and found a gun in Chen's possession. Prosecutors said Zhang admitted to shooting McKinsey during a later interview, and another firearm was found in the car that he admitted to using during the crime.
Prosecutors also said surveillance video was recovered showing both Chen and Zhang shooting the victim.
Chen and Zhang's murder charges included additional allegations of lying in wait and using a firearm.
Court records show McKinsey's killing came during a contentious divorce with his wife and a custody battle over the couple's three young children. In petitions for restraining orders filed last year, the couple accused each other of physical, emotional and psychological abuse going back more than a decade. McKinsey, who is transgender, alleged that both his wife and her parents were verbally and physically abusive regarding a gender transition he underwent years ago.
RELATED: Dublin man allegedly shot, killed by in-laws suffered anti-trans abuse, court records reveal
In his petition for a protection order, McKinsey alleged that Chen had directed anti-LGBTQ slurs at him and his oldest child.
He also accused his wife of being physically and emotionally abusive during medical procedures related to his transition. He alleged Zhang punched him in the chest while he was recovering from double mastectomy surgery.
McKinsey was arrested last October and charged with misdemeanor child abuse for allegedly hitting their oldest son. Police said he acknowledged having slapped the child. Prosecutors also charged him with endangering their youngest child after deputies responded to the family’s home to talk with him and found their 2-year-old had been left home alone, according to court documents.
RELATED: Documents reveal child abuse, domestic violence claims of Dublin man allegedly killed by in-laws
McKinsey pleaded not guilty to the charges and alleged in court records that he had been set up by his wife, who had left the house without telling him the child was sleeping in a crib upstairs. He was released from jail on the condition that he complete 12 parenting classes. At the time of his killing, McKinsey was out on bail and had been trying to enter a mental health diversion program.
It was also in October that McKinsey's wife obtained a domestic violence protection order against McKinsey.
The wife said in her filing that in 2010 McKinsey had grabbed her by the forearms during one argument and caused her to hit the corner of a coffee table, fracturing a vertebra in her upper back. She also said that in 2023 she called the police to their home after McKinsey pushed their oldest son hard on the head. The wife also accused McKinsey of emotionally abusing her mother.
McKinsey in December filed his own request for domestic violence protection against his wife, alleging years of abuse that included her hitting him in the head with a frying pan. He later filed for divorce and sought more time with the three children, noting that he had been limited to two hours of supervised visits per week since last fall, Alameda County court documents show.
In late August, McKinsey was granted unsupervised visits in public twice a week.
The killing occurred a week before a hearing was scheduled in McKinsey and his wife’s divorce case. The couple had been married since July 2011.
McKinsey joined The New York Times in January 2023. He was director of engineering for New York Times Games and based in the San Francisco Bay Area, the paper said. A spokesperson declined to comment further.
ABC7 Eyewitness News contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: White Sox 7, Astros 3: A postseason series victory
articles.title_zh: White Sox 7, Astros 3: A postseason series victory
articles.content_orig:
7:46 PM CDT on September 30, 2026
Erick Fedde celebrates the final out.
In the 57 years Major League Baseball has made it possible to win a postseason series without winning the World Series, the White Sox had only one one in one season -- 2005, when they won the whole thing.
That count is up to two, and this series ended the same as the last one, with the White Sox sealing a sweep in Houston's ballpark.
The White Sox knocked Hunter Brown out of the first inning with a four-run blitz, and when three Astros solo shots narrowed the margin to one, Chase Meidroth regained the ground in the sixth inning with a resounding three-run blast off Bryan Abreu. The White Sox bullpen, which wobbled out of the gate, ended up throwing five scoreless innings to exit Houston as victors.
Meidroth's clout will probably stand as the defining image of this series, especially since the White Sox barely escaped the previous inning with the lead intact.
Huascar Brazobán entered in relief of Sean Burke with a 4-3 lead in the fifth inning and promptly plunked Cam Smith. He struck out Nick Allen to gain some footing, but a single to Jeremy Peña brought Yordan Alvarez to the plate without a base open.
Will Venable countered with Anthony Kay, who fell behind 3-0 ... and still got him out, spotting an outside-corner fastball that Alvarez sliced to Sam Antonacci in left for the second out. Kay then fell behind Isaac Paredes and walked him on four pitches to load the bases. Jose Altuve, who hit one of the three homers off Burke earlier in the game, made Kay throw a fastball strike, but got a well-located changeup on the second pitch, and flied out to right to strand three.
That provided temporary relief, but the White Sox now had to solve their problems on offense, which ground to a halt once Brown left the game. Antonacci grounded out with the bases loaded to start a streak of 13 consecutive batters retired by AJ Blubaugh and Peter Lambert, the prospective Game 3 starter who ended up taking over in the third.
The Sox finally snapped the streak when Andrew Benintendi took a full-count fastball low for a leadoff walk in the top of the sixth. Luisangel Acuña pinch-ran for him and stole second, although the effects were negated when Tristan Peters walked on four pitches. That's when Joe Espada went to the bullpen for his top right-handed reliever, Bryan Abreu, to face Chase Meidroth.
Initially, the White Sox were going to concede the matchup as Meidroth showed bunt on Abreu's first pitch. But Acuña and Peters took off on Abreu's first pitch, which nobody on the Astros anticipated for the kind of incredibly easy double steal the White Sox have been used to allowing. That allowed Meidroth to swing away, and did he ever.
First, he watched two more pitches out of the zone to make it a 3-0 count. He took all the way on a fastball strike, and when Abreu went to the slider on 3-1, Abreu left it over the inner half, and Meidroth uncoiled on it, sending it off the left field wall above the yellow line for a three-run blast that set the White Sox dugout ablaze and allowed White Sox fans to breathe a huge sigh of relief.
Thanks to Jordan Hicks and Erick Fedde, blood pressures remained settled the rest of the evening. Hicks retired all six batters he faced to go 10-for-10 over the two games, and Fedde did the same as the unlikely final pitcher.
The sweep indicated how thoroughly the White Sox outplayed the Astros. Brown came into this game 6-0 in six starts against Chicago, but thanks to a series of line drives and miscues, he departed with only two outs in the first and trailing 4-0.
Sam Antonacci started the game by exploiting a compromised Astros defense. Houston started Alvarez in left field due to Paredes' knee issue, and Antonacci lined a drive over his outstretched glove in left center for a leadoff double. Kyle Teel then shot a single past a diving Altuve, and the White Sox had a 1-0 lead in just five pitches.
Miguel Vargas followed with a bouncer to third, but Nick Allen's attempt to smother the hop deflected off him and into foul territory for an E-5. Brown rebounded to strike out Munetaka Murakami, but Andrew Benintendi picked him up with a broken-bat single to center that scored Teel, and then Vargas when an ill-advised throw from center escaped catcher Yainer Diaz. Tristan Peters then got on top of a high fastball for a single to right center that scored Benintendi to make it 4-0.
Brown gave up a single to Meidroth and struck out Braden Montgomery to bring up ninth-hitting Colson Montgomery, but a walk turned over the lineup and ended his night. The move worked, as Blubaugh got Antonacci to ground out to avoid an even bigger disaster.
From there, the Astros offense chipped away. Jeremy Peña greeted Burke with a homer to get Houston on the board, Cam Smith hit a bomb in the second, and Altuve made it three over four innings by dropping one in the Crawford Boxes to make it a 4-3 game.
That said, the adage that solo shots won't kill you proved correct enough. Burke allowed only one other hit and zero walks while striking out eight, so while the Astros killed his mistakes, there were no multiplying factors. He didn't quite get the game to the halfway point, but while the Sox used four relievers, everybody will get the next two full days off.
*The final pitching line plays: 9 IP, 5 H, 3 R, 3 ER, 1 BB, 15 K, 3 HR.
*The Sox once again found production without their biggest bats, as Vargas and Murakami went 0-for-10 with five strikeouts in the middle of the order.
*The Sox were 4-for-9 with runners in scoring position, while the Astros were 0-for-2. They won both the denominator and the numerator.
*The Sox also played errorless ball, with Vargas making up for his Game 1 error by stabbing an Alvarez hot shot as the only defender on the left side.
*Alvarez finished the series 1-for-8 with two strikeouts.

The adaptation of John Steinbeck’s literary masterpiece took center stage at the Plaza Hotel’s New York premiere. The Netflix series offers a fresh interpretation of John Steinbeck’s 1952 novel, East of Eden , shifting its focus to the story’s antihero, Cathy Ames.
In the titular role of Ames, Florence Pugh stars in the series with an ensemble featuring Christopher Abbott, Mike Faist, Hoon Lee, Tracy Letts, Ciarán Hinds, Martha Plimpton, Joseph Zada, and Joe Anders.
Zoe Kazan serves as the writer, co-showrunner and executive producer, alongside co-showrunner and executive producer Jeb Stuart. Kazan’s grandfather directed the 1955 film adaptation of the novel, East of Eden , starring James Dean in his first major leading role.
Steinbeck’s classic is an epic multigenerational saga set in California’s Salinas Valley between the American Civil War and World War I. At its core, the novel is a modern retelling of the Biblical story of Cain and Abel, exploring free will, parental rejection, and the eternal battle between good and evil.

Inside the walls of Fort Dix federal prison in New Jersey, no one is living quite like inmate #37452-054.
There are men who cook for him and men who clean for him. There are men who make his bed and men who do his laundry. There is even a man who gives him Chinese-style massages.
This is how Sean “Diddy” Combs has been living in prison, according to four men who have spent time in the same unit as the disgraced hip-hop mogul. They were granted anonymity to speak freely about life inside the prison.
“This is not some normal s--- you see in jail. This is some rich s---,” said one of the men. “It looks crazy, but again, it’s Diddy.”
This story is also drawn in part from photos and videos taken inside the prison and reviewed by NBC News. They include footage of Combs appearing to use a contraband phone.
Diddy appears to use cellphone in prison
Combs, 56, is serving a 50-month sentence for prostitution-related offenses. But he is still living a privileged life, the sources said, and it’s not just because of the inmates willing to perform even the most basic tasks for him for the right price.
Multiple sources said he uses contraband cellphones to scroll Instagram and scan nude and sexually explicit photos that an old girlfriend sends him. He’s been able to buy from other inmates an antidepressant drug sought out for its mood-boosting effects — Remeron, or “rem-roms” as they are known in prison. On weekend nights, he’d often tap into a secret stash of premium liquor, which would be smuggled in by guards and shared with a tight group of fellow inmates.
“Hell yeah, I drank with him,” said one of the men, who recounted drinking Hennessy with Combs.
A spokesperson for Combs downplayed the details of his prison life.
“The continued scrutiny of every mundane detail of Sean Combs’s life in prison has reached the point where the media characterizes ordinary prison life as news,” the spokesperson said. “The only real news is that Sean continues to serve his sentence while awaiting the court’s decision on his appeal.”
A Bureau of Prisons spokesperson said the agency does not comment on a particular inmate’s conditions due to “privacy, safety and security reasons.”
“Like all correctional agencies, contraband, particularly cell phones, narcotics, and weapons, remains a constant challenge, and we continue to tackle the problem of contraband being introduced into our facilities,” the spokesperson added in a statement.
Combs’ exalted existence behind bars doesn’t come cheap.
He has spent thousands of dollars a month to bring his lifestyle to the low-security prison, sources said, with the money flowing from people outside prison to the commissary accounts of those inmates performing services for him.
Those paid by Combs include a man who would clean the toilet and shower areas before he’d use them, and men who would secretly cook him special meals — curry chicken, pizza, empanadas — using a makeshift heating element submerged in water, sources said.
“After a while, I got tired of cooking,” said one man who described preparing meals for Combs and other inmates. “He started going to the Jamaicans.”
There are also inmates who hold on to Combs’ phone and fan mail for him.
“It’s so much that he gets,” one of the sources said. “He doesn’t have room for it.”
Like many other state and federal prisons across the U.S., Fort Dix has grappled with a contraband problem . Just last week, five people, including a current and former corrections officer, were charged with running a scheme to smuggle illicit items into the South Jersey prison. The contraband included knives, marijuana and cellphones, federal prosecutors said.
Since 2020, authorities have also charged multiple people for allegedly using drones to drop illicit goods into the Fort Dix prison yard or atop a roof . The suspects have included inmates and outside accomplices who had previously served time at the facility. In one case, Fort Dix staff intercepted a 46-pound laundry bag filled with contraband.
Combs isn’t the first famous person to receive special treatment behind bars. Harvey Weinstein, for one, was held in a private room at the Rikers Island jail in New York, with access to his own phone, bathroom and television, according to The City Reporter .
The massive Fort Dix prison, 60 miles southwest of New York City, houses about 4,000 inmates.
Combs arrived there in October following his conviction on two counts of transporting people across state lines for sexual encounters.
The trial featured lurid testimony about highly choreographed sexual encounters Combs organized called “freak offs.” They involved male sex workers, elaborate costumes, drugs and former girlfriends — including the singer Cassie — who filed a lawsuit against Combs alleging years of physical and sexual abuse. (The case was settled, with Combs denying any wrongdoing.)
His trial ended in a split verdict, with a New York jury finding him not guilty on sex trafficking and racketeering charges that could have put him in prison for life.
Following his sentencing, Combs’ lawyers pushed for him to be sent to Fort Dix in part because it offers a drug treatment program. Completing the monthslong program often leads to a reduction of an inmate’s prison term, making it highly coveted.
Combs entered the program upon his arrival at Fort Dix. Sources said it took little time for him to acquire a phone, alcohol and a growing number of inmates on his payroll.
“Pretty much the day he arrived, the party started,” one of the sources said.
Many Fort Dix inmates consume alcohol and Remeron, sources said. The medication is prescribed to inmates suffering from depression and anxiety. But it’s also bought and sold on the prison’s robust black market, the sources said.
“You can pretty much get anything except a key to the front door and a female,” one of the sources said.
Among the items Combs has gotten his hands on, two sources said, is a “jailbroken” tablet that he has used to watch movies and documentaries — including “Sean Combs: The Reckoning,” the Netflix docuseries produced by his longtime nemesis 50 Cent.
His presence at the prison has also led to some surreal moments, the sources said. In his first few days, he would walk around in only a towel or boxer shorts after a shower, prompting inmates to warn him that he could be targeted for sex.
“That’s not normal,” one of the sources said.
Over the summer Combs was placed in solitary confinement following a fight with another inmate, NBC News reported in July . He was later kicked out of the drug treatment program, sources said.
But after he was moved out of solitary, the sources said, he went right back to living the life great wealth can buy you in prison, with a team of inmates catering to him.
“He’s a billionaire. People are in awe of him,” said one of the sources. “Money is power, especially behind bars.”
Rich Schapiro is a reporter with the NBC News national security unit.
Chloe Melas is an entertainment correspondent for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: BBC paying to air shows like Suits and Schitt's Creek is illogical, MPs say
articles.title_zh: BBC paying to air shows like Suits and Schitt's Creek is illogical, MPs say
articles.content_orig:
The BBC should not pay "over the odds" for the rights to overseas hits such as Suits and Schitt's Creek, an influential group of MPs has said.
It is one of several issues raised in a wide-ranging report about the BBC's funding and future, published by the House of Commons' cross-party culture and media committee.
Although the BBC produces a lot of its own programmes, the corporation buys some international shows for its TV channels and iPlayer streaming platform.
The MPs' report said the BBC could "spend more wisely when competing for programming". Overall, the BBC brings "immeasurable benefits" to society but needs reform of the TV licence fee to avoid a fate of "managed decline", they said.
Committee chair Dame Caroline Dinenage said the report comes at "a pivotal moment for the BBC", which is grappling with changing media habits, declining income and negotiations with the government over how it is paid for.
Dame Caroline said the government "must ensure the BBC has a universal and sustainable source of funding".
But, she added, the BBC "can play its part by sweating its assets and boxing clever for the licence payer by ending illogical practices such as outbidding commercial rivals for overseas hits such as Suits, Schitt's Creek and Scooby Doo".
The rights to air all three programmes were bought by the BBC after contracts with other networks or streaming services expired.
"At a time of constrained resources, the BBC should not be paying over the odds for overseas content, particularly when it's a bidding war against commercial UK broadcasters," the committee said.
The MPs added that they "did not believe that this provides value for money for the licence fee payer".
The BBC said it spends less than 5% of its content budget on acquiring shows, less than other broadcasters, and they are a cost-effective way of delivering high-quality content to audiences who go on to discover homegrown programming.
The committee's report has been published as the government considers its options for the next BBC Royal Charter, which will set out how the broadcaster will be governed, regulated and funded from 2028 onwards.
Dame Caroline said: "For all its faults, the BBC drives our creative economy, supports our democracy through media sovereignty, and delivers world-class entertainment and moments that bring us together.
"Like a much-loved family member, we may criticise and grumble about the BBC but we would miss it enormously if it were no longer here for us."
The committee said there were "considerable challenges" for the BBC and warned that the current TV licence fee is "outdated and no longer fit for purpose".
Currently, about 94% of individuals use the BBC each month but only 80% of households pay for a TV licence, the MPs noted.
"The licence fee should be reformed so it is no longer linked to the consumption of live TV or to a particular device, such as a television set," the committee said.
"This should be an easier sell to licence fee payers if expanding the base is paired with a drop in the individual cost."
The BBC's director-general Matt Brittin has previously described the current licence fee model as "a busted flush" and "yesterday's model", and has said the price could be cut if more people pay under an overhauled system.
The committee also suggested the BBC should:
The committee suggested the government should:
The committee supported opening up BBC iPlayer to shows from other public service broadcasters such as Channel 4.
Earlier this week, Channel 4 chief executive Priya Dogra said she was open to her network's content being hosted on iPlayer.
The report also called for the end of political appointments to the BBC board, to improve governance and remain trusted by the public.
And the committee recommended that the BBC is given new public purposes relating to innovation and technology and combating misinformation and disinformation.
The BBC welcomed the report, which it said made "some important and interesting recommendations on the future of the BBC".
A BBC spokesperson said: "We have consistently argued that the current funding model is outdated and needs reform, so we welcome the Committee's support for maintaining universal funding while overhauling the licence fee.
"We are also pleased to see their recognition of the vital work of the World Service, with a clear recommendation that responsibility for funding should return fully to Government.
"At a time of huge disruption in the media, the BBC's trust, reach and creative strength remain unparalleled. But we also recognise the need to evolve and move faster towards the future."
The government's Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) said it "agrees entirely with the Committee's conclusion that it is in the country's best interests for the next Charter to support an ambitious and innovative BBC, and that the corporation cannot be left to a future of managed decline".
A DCMS spokesperson added: "We will review and consider the committee's recommendations in detail, alongside the views of the public and other stakeholders, to inform decisions for the next Royal Charter."

articles.title_orig: Swiss glaciers suffer 'disastrous' year of ice loss, threatening water supplies
articles.title_zh: Swiss glaciers suffer 'disastrous' year of ice loss, threatening water supplies
articles.content_orig:
Swiss glaciers have suffered a near-record loss of ice in 2026, new data shows, as intense summer heatwaves take their toll on Alpine peaks.
More than 5% of the country's remaining glacier ice has disappeared in the last 12 months, which scientists say is "extraordinary".
They warn that such rapid melting is no longer a surprise given the pace of climate change, but it could threaten water supplies for farming, hydropower and transport in the decades ahead.
The loss of glacier ice can also destabilise mountain slopes and increase the risk of landslides in some places - which can lead to flash flooding in extreme cases, as seen in Nepal in August.
There were multiple factors involved in that event, which was triggered when a large area of bedrock and glacier ice collapsed.
But scientists say long-term glacier thinning and the thawing of frozen ground likely raised the risks.
The notable finding from this latest report is not so much that Swiss glaciers are shrinking - which is to be expected in our warming climate, driven primarily by fossil fuel emissions - but the sheer pace of melting.
Until recently, glaciologists in the Alps considered 2% of ice lost in a single year to be "extreme". This year has seen an estimated 5.5% disappear.
"It's really just disastrous," said Dr Matthias Huss, director of Glacier Monitoring Switzerland, which produced the report.
Swiss glaciers started the summer in an already difficult place, covered by less snow than usual after a mild winter.
And much of that snow disappeared quickly in the early and intense heatwaves of May and June , exposing the glacier ice below.
Bare ice is darker and less reflective than fresh snow, so absorbs more of the Sun's energy.
That left glaciers vulnerable to melting even faster in subsequent heatwaves.
"Ten years ago, I wouldn't have thought that it's possible to lose glaciers so quickly," said Dr Fabien Maussion, a glaciologist at the University of Bristol, who was not involved in the Swiss report.
"What's happened over the summer now is extremely distressing… but at the same time it was to be expected from a climate scientist's perspective," he added.
Meltwater from glaciers can be an important source of water for irrigation, hydropower and even shipping traffic during hot, dry conditions.
Scientists estimate that Swiss glaciers released 2.2 trillion litres of meltwater between July and September.
Although that helped to ease water shortages this summer, it has rapidly diminished the frozen supply.
The loss of ice could pose long-term challenges, Huss warned, with smaller glaciers unable to top up water levels to the same extent.
"Every drop of water that runs off during these heatwaves is kind of old water that's been stocked in the glacier ice centuries or decades ago," said Huss.
"It's helping us [now] but it's unsustainable, so we won't have it at [our] disposal in the next heatwave."
The River Rhine reached record lows in places this summer , affecting shipping navigation routes and increasing transport costs.
One of the most ominous findings is what researchers observed at measurement sites at the highest elevations, where temperatures are lowest and glaciers are typically snow-covered.
Even as high as 3,500 metres above sea level, scientists found no snow remaining at the end of summer.
"At some glaciers we've seen four metres of ice loss at the highest point, where they should be covered by several metres of winter snow at this time of the year," said Huss, from Glacier Monitoring Switzerland.
Snow is like glacier food - and under stable conditions some of it would eventually compact into ice.
But if no snow survives the summer, it cannot replace the ice lost to melting at lower, warmer elevations. The glacier will starve, shrink and eventually disappear.
"Glaciers are complex because they gain mass at the top and they flow downstream, so there is a lot of physics," explained Maussion.
"But in its simplest form, what we see right now is that we took an ice cube out of the fridge and it's just melting in front of our eyes."
Scientists say the climate is now too warm for many Alpine glaciers to survive.
Some, like Plattalva in eastern Switzerland, have already disappeared.
But researchers stress that sharp cuts to carbon emissions can still save much of the world's glacier ice.
This is particularly the case for the Himalayas and the polar regions, where most of the planet's ice resides.
"There we still can make a big difference with protecting the climate," said Huss.
"If these ice masses can be saved or stabilised, we can limit the rise of global sea levels… which could affect billions of people living along the coast."

articles.title_orig: OpenAI links China’s Moonshot AI to attempt to extract its models’ reasoning
articles.title_zh: OpenAI links China’s Moonshot AI to attempt to extract its models’ reasoning
articles.content_orig:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman declined an invitation to appear at a Senate subcommittee hearing on Wednesday on the risks of rogue artificial intelligence , according to Sen. Josh Hawley , R-Mo.
Hawley, who chairs the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs subpanel that held the hearing, sent a letter to Altman on Sept. 25 requesting his presence to "help shed light on the Subcommittee's ongoing investigation into recent rogue AI incidents involving OpenAI models." NBC News first reported that Altman did not accept the invitation to testify.
"He turned us down," Hawley said of Altman at the hearing. "I think that's unfortunate because I think the American people deserve to know exactly what's going on at all of these companies. And to give us the sort of transparency that I think is needed for not just comfort, but to have an understanding of what these companies — that are the most powerful companies in the world — are doing right now with the most powerful technology ever known to man."
A spokesperson for OpenAI noted that Altman received the invitation to testify on Friday, just five days ahead of the hearing. Altman on Tuesday appeared at the company's annual DevDay developer conference in San Francisco as other AI officials — including OpenAI President Greg Brockman — were in Washington meeting with President Donald Trump.
"OpenAI is deeply engaged with Congress on federal policies to advance AI safety, including through dozens of meetings in recent weeks with members of both parties in both chambers," the spokesperson said. "We look forward to continuing to work constructively and proactively with Senator Hawley and members of Congress on federal AI safety legislation that materially raises the safety bar."
Hawley's overture to Altman comes weeks after he opened an investigation into OpenAI earlier this month. Hawley sought information on a cyberattack involving hundreds of OpenAI agents that broke out of their testing sandbox and hacked into the systems of another AI company called Hugging Face.
The cyber attack was one in a series of recent hacks involving frontier AI models that have raised alarms and prompted calls for Congress to act to rein in the rapidly evolving technology.
Hawley requested information from Altman on the cyber attack and on the existential risks of the technology and set an Oct. 1 deadline. A spokesperson for Hawley said OpenAI is expected to provide additional documents by the end of the week.
"The American people deserve to know the details of what went on in the Hugging Face incident and other incidents of AI models going rogue.  This investigation will seek those answers," Hawley said in the Sept. 10 letter.

articles.title_orig: Trump hails the US military’s exit from Iraq after 12-year mission against Islamic State
articles.title_zh: Trump hails the US military’s exit from Iraq after 12-year mission against Islamic State
articles.content_orig:
The United States announced it had completed its withdrawal from Iraq on Wednesday, more than 20 years after invading the country to topple Saddam Hussein, in a move that was celebrated by the Iraqi government and the Pentagon – as well as Iran and its allies, who claim years of pressure forced the American departure.
The long-planned withdrawal was completed after US troops left their last remaining bases in Erbil , northern Iraq, and comes amid the ongoing war between the US and neighboring Iran.
“This milestone reflects the success of a 12-year campaign that defeated ISIS as an organized military threat in Iraq and across the region,” Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said in a statement. “It also marks a transition from a wartime coalition mission to an Iraqi-led security effort supported by a more normal bilateral security relationship.”
One Iranian-supported militia , As’hab Al-Kahf, cheered the US exit, congratulating Iraqis “on the humiliating withdrawal of the American occupier under the strikes of the Resistance’s drones and missiles.”
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi presided over the handover ceremony and described the US withdrawal as the beginning of a “a new phase, one defined by Iraq’s sovereignty, the strength of its institutions, the readiness of its forces, the unity of its decision-making, and balanced partnerships with its friends.”
In 2024, the Iraqi government and the Biden administration agreed to a phased withdrawal of US troops, a plan the Trump administration has honored. The pullout, however, leaves a new Iraqi government with the daunting task of loosening Iran’s grip on its neighbor, which has long been trapped in a cycle of sectarianism, foreign meddling and civil conflict.
“The Iran-backed groups viewed the US presence an extension of the occupation of Iraq,” Lahib Higel, deputy program director for the Middle East and North Africa at International Crisis Group, told CNN. “These groups believe that the US were in Iraq to monitor the activities of the Iran-allied militias,” she added.
Saudi Arabia braces for attacks on ports and airports by Iraqi militias working with Iran-backed Houthis
At its height, the US had 170,000 troops in Iraq before the Obama administration withdrew the forces from the country in 2011. About 5,000 troops were deployed to Iraq in 2014 at the request of the Iraqi government, which sought US assistance in the fight against ISIS. Since December 2021, the US has had roughly 2,500 troops in Iraq in an advise and assist capacity, working to train Iraqi military to fight ISIS.
The American presence in Iraq spanned more than two decades and several missions. The last of them, a 12-year campaign against ISIS, sought to dismantle the Sunni extremist group that carved out territory across Syria and Iraq in the mid-2010s. When war widened between Israel and Iran-aligned factions from Gaza to Yemen, US troops in Iraq became frequent targets of Tehran’s proxy militias.
Military and intelligence officials discuss smaller presence in the Middle East as US looks for another post-9/11 strategy
Strikes on US bases and troops rose further this year after President Donald Trump launched a war with Iran that killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, a figure Iranian loyalist militias revered as the head of the armed resistance.
The primary responsibility for addressing Iraq’s “remaining security challenges” including ISIS and Iran-aligned militias “now rests” with the Iraqi government, Parnell said in the statement.
The US withdrawal comes as several regional governments launch efforts to disarm Iran’s powerful militias, who have grown powerful with political, financial and military influence within Arab countries.
For three years, Iran has been losing influence in key areas across the Middle East. Lebanon’s Hezbollah was severely weakened by an Israeli invasion into southern Lebanese villages, and the fall of Iran’s ally in Syria, Bashar al-Assad , has forced Iranian groups to concede strategic territory.
Iran is turning to Iraq to hold onto a network of allied politicians, militias and media outlets. Even as its position has eroded in other arenas, the US pullout has left Iran-aligned groups feeling victorious and newly empowered.
Still, Iraq’s new prime minister, Ali al-Zaidi, has pledged “no weapon outside the umbrella of the law, and no force outside the state’s institutions.”
Experts, including Higel, are doubtful that the Iraqi government will be able to disarm the Iran-loyal groups even if war between Iran and the US ends.
“It’s quite an impossible task to quickly disarm these groups,” Higel said. “For as long as the regime stands in Tehran, it would be very difficult to imagine that the groups would lay down their arms.”
After first treating the US military withdrawal as a condition for laying down their arms, the groups have since piled on new demands and refused to disarm, putting them on a collision course with the Iraqi state.
“We believe the disarmament demand is American, Zionist, Western, and Gulf-backed, aimed at weakening Iraq,” a leading commander of a powerful Iranian militia in Iraq, Harakat al-Nujaba, told CNN. “There has to be a withdrawal of the occupation in all its forms and guises - American, Western, and Turkish - and the liberation of political, economic, military, and security decision-making.”
The commander requested anonymity to speak freely to CNN. Harakat al-Nujaba is a US-designated Foreign Terror Organization.
Iran’s proxies have proven useful in adding pressure on Washington’s allies in the region. This month, Iraqi groups loyal to Iran fired drones on a vital Saudi oil pipeline, disrupting global crude supply and leaving oil prices soaring.
“The issue of surrendering weapons is a delusion harbored by the weak, the humiliated, and the dollar’s slaves,” the Iranian proxy Ashab Al-Kahf said in a statement at the time. “We will continue participating in the resistance axis as ordered by the (Islamic Republic of Iran’s) religious authority.”

articles.title_orig: Micron Profit, Revenue Surge as Memory Crunch Looks to Last Through 2028
articles.title_zh: Micron Profit, Revenue Surge as Memory Crunch Looks to Last Through 2028
articles.content_orig:
Micron reported better-than-expected quarterly results on Wednesday as the memory maker continues to benefit from soaring demand for AI infrastructure. The stock rose slightly in extended trading.
Here's how the company did relative to LSEG consensus:
Revenue almost quadrupled in the fiscal fourth quarter from $11.32 billion a year earlier, according to a statement .
For the fiscal first quarter, Micron said it expects revenue of about $61.5 billion and adjusted earnings per share of $38.15. Analysts polled by LSEG had expected $35.40 in adjusted earnings per share on $57 billion in revenue.
Micron's stock has soared more than 500% in the past year, benefiting from a worldwide supply crunch caused by historic levels of demand for memory chips needed for artificial intelligence models and workloads. The shortage has led to a spike in memory costs and resulted in increased prices for  consumer electronics like Apple 's iPads and MacBooks.
Hendi Susanto, portfolio at Gabelli Funds, said in an email after the release that it was "another strong beat and raise for Micron."
"At this point, I have not heard any negative data points pointing to the memory cycle reversing toward a decline anytime soon for the foreseeable future," Susanto wrote.
Micron is the only U.S.-based maker of high-bandwidth memory, HBM, made up of stacks of general-purpose dynamic random-access memory, or DRAM. Fourth-quarter DRAM revenue increased 343% from a year ago to $39.8 billion, representing 73% of total sales.
CEO Sanjay Mehrotra said on the earnings call that the company has a "strong roadmap for future HBM products" and is working with Nvidia on the industry's "first custom HBM implementation."
Net income in the latest quarter climbed to $37.7 billion, or $32.87 per share, from $3.2 billion, or $2.83 per share a year ago.
Advanced graphics and central processors from chip giants like Nvidia and AMD need increasing amounts of HBM to handle AI workloads, and the world's leading providers can't make enough.
That's why Micron is investing $250 billion to build two new campuses for making HBM. The largest broke ground in Clay, New York, in January, while its first new fab in Boise, Idaho, is scheduled to come online next year.
HBM leaders SK Hynix and Samsung are also in the midst of massive new HBM factory buildouts in their home country of South Korea. Micron holds the smallest HBM market share of the three, but its market cap has still topped $1.2 trillion.
Mehrotra participated in a summit on AI regulation hosted by President Donald Trump on Tuesday, days after attending a White House dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping on his first visit to the U.S. in more than a decade.
On the call, Mehrotra said Micron increased compensation for every employee in fiscal 2026. Hundreds of Micron staffers threatened to strike at its factories in Taiwan over labor negotiations and pay. Similar strikes at rivals SK Hynix and Samsung have result in bonuses upwards of $500,000 .

articles.title_orig: Hundreds of Catholic Clerics Abused Children in Massachusetts, Report Says
articles.title_zh: Hundreds of Catholic Clerics Abused Children in Massachusetts, Report Says
articles.content_orig:
Attorney General Andrea Campbell had just delivered findings from a report on previously undisclosed child sexual abuse perpetrated by the Catholic clergy — adding more horrific stories and disconcerting numbers to one of the darkest, most painful subjects in Massachusetts history.
Then, the state’s highest law enforcement official issued one last startling revelation: She, too, is a survivor of childhood sexual abuse.
“For me to stand up here, it would be absolutely inauthentic, and inauthentic to my faith, to not share that I am a survivor of childhood abuse,” she said, adding it was “not at the hands of the church, but at the hands of a relative.”
While she did not disclose other details, including the identity of her abuser or when it occurred, Campbell said she decided to come forward after her office had for years investigated the clergy and after hearing firsthand the trauma other victims suffered.
“Frankly, my faith has allowed me to overcome that,” said Campbell, 44.
The first-term attorney general disclosed that abuse at a news conference Wednesday addressing an investigation from her office that found nearly 1,000 children had been abused by hundreds of clergy members across three Catholic dioceses.
Producing the 200-plus-page report , she said, was a “very difficult investigation for every team member that was a part of it.” Her office reviewed more than 300,000 pages of records and interviewed more than 100 people since 2019, Campbell said, speaking with survivors and their attorneys, clergy members, and experts in child sex abuse, among others.
Campbell is not the only Massachusetts official to disclose they have been the victim of abuse. In attendance Wednesday  were state Senator Joan Lovely and state Representative John Lawn, both of whom have said they, too, endured childhood sexual abuse and have pushed legislation to address it.
Lawn, a Watertown Democrat, filed legislation to eliminate the state’s civil statute of limitations on childhood sexual abuse. The House passed a version of that proposal as part of a wider primary care bill, which is in closed-door negotiations between legislative leaders.
“Trauma does not operate on a legal timeline,” Lawn wrote in a Globe op-ed in May. “It can take years to recognize what happened, decades to speak it aloud, and a lifetime to fully understand the harm — not only inflicted by abusers but also enabled by the institutions around them.”
Lovely, meanwhile, called the release of the report an “incredibly powerful moment” that could help further the Legislature’s work on the issue. The issue, the Salem Democrat said, is “personal.”
“As the attorney general has revealed her past, it brings that compassion that really can help survivors,” said Lovely.
The first woman of color to hold statewide office in Massachusetts, Campbell has regularly talked about the tragedies and family struggles that have marked her personal life while in the public eye.
Her father was arrested when she was just months old; her mother was killed in a car accident months later. She lived with a mix of relatives and foster parents for years before her father returned when she was 8. Her twin brother, Andre, faced criminal charges in multiple cases and died in custody before age 30. Her estranged brother, Alvin, was convicted of a string of rapes and sentenced this year to life in prison .
Campbell, meanwhile, graduated from Princeton University, and then UCLA Law School. She ultimately became a Boston city councilor, ran for mayor in 2021 , and then won the attorney general’s office four years ago.
Throughout, she has been open about her religious conviction, referencing it in many ways: Campbell has long spoken of turning to gospel music or her Bible in hard times, noting she prays daily, and has said she has “ an unwavering faith in a God who will not only see me through, but also this Commonwealth.”
“We can respect faith communities while also demanding accountability from the very institutions we give our trust,” Campbell said. “This investigation was not about demonizing a faith or a church. Rather, it was about seeking justice, a value, and a promise our faith and the God I serve so deeply reflects.”
Campbell added Wednesday that others in her office, too, came forward about their own past trauma after “looking at the revelation of this report.” It made the work, she said, “personal for so many folks on a deeper level, and for many, that can be very traumatic.”
Nonetheless, she stressed Wednesday that the work of her office isn’t done and encouraged others to come forward and share any allegations of abuse.
“To survivors whose courage made this investigation possible, we not only hear you and see you, we absolutely love you,” Campbell said. “I will stand in my faith every single day, standing for what it actually means and what it actually stands for and should demonstrate: Love, connection, and justice.”

articles.title_orig: ASU hockey coach is put on leave; hospitalized player is unlikely to recover, family attorney says
articles.title_zh: ASU hockey coach is put on leave; hospitalized player is unlikely to recover, family attorney says
articles.content_orig:
Arizona State University announced Wednesday it has put hockey coach Greg Powers on leave following the collapse of player Matthew Mayich during a summer team workout. Mayich, 21, remains on life support and is unlikely to recover, according to family attorney Rob Carey.
In response to the announcement, Carey said in an interview with “NBC Nightly News” that the family has said “since day one” that the entire coaching staff needed to be put on administrative leave. ASU has left in place another assistant coach who is good friends with the head coach “and that needs to change,” the attorney said.
“They did nothing right, literally nothing,” Carey said of the ASU coaching staff during the workout. “And as a result [of] what should have been a very preventable workout problem, heatstroke, a man is on life support and unlikely to come off of it,” he said.
“He’s incapacitated, and there’s almost no chance of recovery. But the family’s very devout, and they want to give their son a chance for a miracle,” Carey said.
A spokesperson for the university said Wednesday that ASU police have an open and ongoing investigation.
In its announcement on Powers’ leave, ASU athletic director Graham Rossini stated that the school’s “focus continues to be on Matthew and his family” and all student-athletes, to make sure they have “the support they need during this time and as the season begins.”
“We have continued to collect as much information as possible. After thorough and careful deliberation, I believe this is the best move to provide stability for the hockey program,” Rossini said.
Assistant coach Mike Corbett will lead the team this weekend for the season opener, and an interim head coach will be named soon, according to the statement.
Mayich collapsed during an outdoor workout on Aug. 20. He suffered extreme heatstroke and has been hospitalized since his collapse.
Mayich’s parents, John and Christina Mayich, and seven other players from the hockey team called on Tuesday for coaches involved to be placed on leave and for an independent investigation.
The seven players, who did not share their names, submitted through their attorney a letter to ASU President Michael Crow disputing the school’s account of what occurred.
In the letter, the players said they were afraid of being retaliated against because the coaches “decide our playing time, scholarship levels, and roster status.”
Although Carey said putting Powers on leave is a step in the right direction, he said there are players whose safety remains at risk and “retaliation is still possible.”
The athletes’ 26-page letter describes a workout session led by Tim Ziesel, an Army veteran and former Green Beret, on a day the afternoon high temperature was 104 degrees and the low was 74, according to National Weather Service data. The players alleged in their letter that Ziesel left before Mayich collapsed.
According to the players, the workout did not include required emergency gear on site, including a tub of water for cooling off, and a training plan had not been submitted to all the coaches.
In its report, ASU said temperatures were between 86 and 89 degrees during the workout, with relative humidity between 51% and 46%. The ASU report also stated that an athletic trainer evaluated Mayich’s condition, put cool water and iced towels on him and told him to stay down; she then called 911 and directed student-athletes to help move him to the shade.
Buddy Rake, Ziesel’s attorney, said Ziesel has offered to meet privately with Mayich’s family “and thinks a full and complete investigation should be done.”
“You have to find out what caused this. At the same time this workout is occurring, there’s probably 5,000 high school athletes in Arizona doing the same workout, and nothing happens to them. So either the protocol is wrong, or there’s something else that happened,” Rake said.
The players’ letter alleges the university’s temperature and humidity figures “understate conditions on the field.”
The players noted that Mayich was new to Arizona, having been in the area for only eight days and having been involved in the hockey program for five. Drafted by the St. Louis Blues, Mayich is from Hamilton, Ontario, according to the NHL .
The players said that Mayich got no water during a break that lasted only seconds, because he was one of several players who did not reach the water on time before they were “pushed directly into the next task.”
The players said Powers characterized Mayich’s condition after his collapse as “just a little heat stroke” of the type he has seen before, according to their letter.
Carey said putting staff on leave and hiring an outside investigator is fundamental when things such as this occur.
In an interview with Canadian Broadcasting Company earlier this month, Mayich’s mother, Christina, said her son “was so excited to come to ASU — he said the facilities are even better live, because we watch it on YouTube and pictures and he just said it’s exciting.”
She said they’re taking her son’s situation “day by day.”
“Anybody who could send prayers for Matthew, it would be greatly appreciated because right now that’s what we need,” Christina Mayich said.
Suzanne Gamboa is a national reporter for NBC News.
Steve Patterson is a correspondent in Los Angeles for NBC News.
David Douglas is a supervising producer for NBC News based in Los Angeles.

articles.title_orig: Why is Hegseth cutting 20 percent of US general and admiral positions?
articles.title_zh: Why is Hegseth cutting 20 percent of US general and admiral positions?
articles.content_orig:
United States Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has announced plans to cut the number of positions in the military reserved for generals and admirals by 20 percent, raising concerns about political interference in the military’s leadership amid strained relations with senior Pentagon officials .
Speaking on Wednesday at the US Marine Corps base in Quantico, Virginia, Hegseth argued that the reduction was “long overdue” and necessary to purge “woke” elements from the US armed forces.
“You can’t change a culture with the same people who enabled it,” he said. “Personnel is policy at every single level.”
He added that “no fatties, no trannies, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals, just warriors” would be allowed in the US armed forces.
“We’ve ended the poisonous culture of risk aversion and empowered leaders at every single level to simply enforce standards,” Hegseth said. “The only focus, as you know, in your formations should be training, readiness, accountability, discipline and lethality. When you pursue those things, you don’t have to walk on eggshells.”
The Pentagon has presented previous cuts as a way to reduce bureaucracy. But analysts say Hegseth’s latest changes may be aimed at sidelining experienced commanders, discouraging dissent and appointing more officers loyal to President Donald Trump to the ranks.
So is the US military too top-heavy, and what could the cuts mean? Here’s what we know.
Citing Pentagon officials, The Associated Press news agency has reported that Hegseth will double the 10 percent reduction in top-ranking personnel ordered last year, bringing the total decrease to 20 percent by January 1, 2027. The plan affects roughly 800 general and admiral positions across the one- to four-star ranks.
Congress sets statutory limits on the number of generals and admirals. A Congressional Research Service report recorded 848 active-duty generals and admirals in September 2025, below the authorised maximum of 857.
Cutting positions does not necessarily mean immediately dismissing everyone occupying them. An official told the Reuters news agency that some roles would be eliminated, while others would be assigned to lower-ranking offices.
The argument for reducing senior ranks predates Hegseth’s tenure, with supporters saying fewer layers of command would reduce administrative work and give officers closer to operations greater authority.
Walter Ladwig, a political scientist specialising in US foreign policy at King’s College London, said there is a credible case for reform. “Since the end of the Cold War, the overall size of the force has declined significantly, but we haven’t seen a corresponding reduction in the number of flag officers,” he told Al Jazeera.
“At the same time, we’ve seen headquarters and staffs proliferate.”
Trump and Hegseth have already fired or pushed into retirement more than two dozen military leaders since Trump took office in January 2025.
Those removed include General Randy George , the US Army’s top uniformed officer, in April, and Admiral Lisa Franchetti, the chief of naval operations, in February 2025. The administration also dismissed the only two women serving as four-star officers, alongside other senior female officers.
In February 2025, Trump also fired Air Force General CQ Brown as chairman of the US Joint Chiefs of Staff as part of a wider shake-up of top military leadership.
Other departures have been of civilian leaders. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigned in late August after reported disagreements over Hegseth’s handling of senior military personnel.
The dismissals, alongside blocked promotions, have raised questions about how the administration selects commanders and whether professional disagreements could jeopardise careers. Robert Ralston, a lecturer in political science and international studies at the University of Birmingham in the United Kingdom, said the proposed reductions should be weighed alongside these earlier decisions.
“These cuts appear to be part of a broader, sustained effort by Hegseth to fill the ranks based on political, rather than meritocratic, considerations,” he told Al Jazeera.
“Politics is driving these decisions, in my view.”
The move comes at a deeply precarious time for the US military, which is embroiled in an unpopular war in Iran with no end in sight. Hegseth’s leadership over the conflict – and the greater US Defense Department – has come under increasing scrutiny.
Democratic Senator Mark Kelly of Arizona criticised Hegseth’s changes at the Pentagon. “The US military doesn’t need more testosterone; it needs better leadership at this point,” Kelly told MS NOW’s Morning Joe programme last week.
“The consequences of firing all these admirals and generals are that we’re losing a portion, a good portion, of a generation of great leadership.”
David Galbreath, professor of war and technology at the University of Bath in the UK, told Al Jazeera that resistance from Congress and military leaders could complicate the changes.
He pointed to the opposition that arose to President Jimmy Carter’s plans to withdraw US ground troops from South Korea as an example of how military and congressional pressure can constrain a president.
“I suspect that, after the election, we are likely to see a much more confrontational Congress with investigations and impeachments of Hegseth,” he said.
Whether that prediction comes true will likely depend on November’s congressional elections and whether the Republican Party retains control of both chambers of Congress.
Hegseth’s tenure at the Pentagon has been marked by controversy and tensions with senior officials. In March 2025, he shared details of forthcoming strikes on Yemen in a Signal chat group which inadvertently included The Atlantic magazine’s editor-in-chief.
A number of US media reports about the dwindling supplies of weapons in the Middle East prompted his department to investigate leaks and restrict journalists’ access earlier this year. The New York Times reported in August that about 50 Joint Staff military and civilian officials had undergone polygraph tests amid growing mistrust inside the Pentagon.
Hegseth has meanwhile made ending what he calls “woke” culture a central priority, introducing new physical fitness requirements and abolishing diversity policies.
Ralston said the combination of dismissals and blocked promotions could damage morale and the military’s future leadership. “His relationship with senior military leaders has been adversarial. His scuttling of promotions has undoubtedly damaged morale and will have long-term consequences for leadership pipelines within the Department of Defense,” he said.
King’s College’s Ladwig also described Hegseth’s relationship with senior Pentagon leaders as unusually confrontational but cautioned against interpreting every proposed cut as a power struggle.
“When a military is under civilian control, it means that the elected government has the right to determine defence priorities and reorganise the armed forces accordingly,” he said.
But Ladwig warned that the changes could encourage officers to hold back their professional recommendations when advising senior politicians. “That might create incentives for military officers to censor themselves rather than provide candid professional military advice, particularly if being politically aligned with the administration is seen as a path to success,” he said.
“This is a very worrisome pathology, and it’s the kind of thing that produces ineffective militaries in dictatorships.”

articles.title_orig: Trump unveils $200 billion South Korean investment in US; Seoul hedges on Alaska pipeline
articles.title_zh: Trump unveils $200 billion South Korean investment in US; Seoul hedges on Alaska pipeline
articles.content_orig:
President Trump announced plans Wednesday for South Korea to invest in exporting natural gas from Alaska, a project long backed by Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, who is in a competitive reelection contest there.
It marks the second time in three days that the president has sought to highlight planned foreign investments in states where Republican Senate candidates are in tight election campaigns. Mr. Trump made a similar Oval Office announcement on Monday for a massive steel plant in Iowa, another state where Republicans are defending a Senate seat.
The project consists of an 807-mile natural gas pipeline connecting Alaska's petroleum-rich North Slope to a liquefied natural gas export terminal in southern Alaska. It will eventually reduce energy costs for the state's residents by providing a reliable and secure supply, the White House said. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said liquefied natural gas could also be exported to Asia.
Officials said during the Oval Office event that building the pipeline will take three years and that exports of liquefied natural gas would begin two years after that — but that was dependent on financing coming through fully.
It was not clear how quickly South Korea's government would approve the project and how much it planned to spend.
The pipeline is part of a series of projects that Mr. Trump said would get nearly $200 billion in South Korean funds, including a power plant in Texas and eight "large-scale" nuclear power plants. Further details on those investments are not clear.
The investment comes from pledges made as part of a 2025 trade deal with South Korea, which included promises of $350 billion in investments in the United States in exchange for lower U.S. tariffs on South Korean cars, auto parts and other products.
Mr. Trump credited his controversial tariff strategy for making the announcement possible, saying, "Our trade agreement with South Korea, they have to invest hundreds of billions of dollars."
The president credited Sullivan during the Oval Office event.
"He's got my ear, and he's had my ear for a long time on Alaska," Mr. Trump said. The president added that "all these energy projects are all mine, and I got 'em done working with Dan Sullivan."
Sullivan said, "the sky is the limit when we get this project done."
"Mr. President, this one is huge for Alaska," Sullivan said, adding that he'd been working on it "relentlessly."
The push to deliver big projects in areas where GOP candidates could use a boost comes as Mr. Trump's approval ratings have sunk to nearly historic lows ahead of midterm elections. Republicans are also contending with voters' historical tendency to reject whichever party controls the White House during the midterms.
Even Mr. Trump himself has begun acknowledging that Republicans could face an uphill climb in their push to retain control of both chambers of Congress after November, but suggests it is because his administration hasn't done enough to promote its accomplishments.
"I've done a very bad job of explaining," the president said during an event in the White House's East Room, which came before the subsequent announcement on the Alaska investment.
He's promised to help rectify that by spending much of the next 30 days on the road, campaigning ahead of the midterms — though he is beginning that swing with trips to Texas, Alabama, Ohio and Nebraska, which are all normally solidly red states.
Sullivan, who has been a persistent advocate for the Alaska natural gas project and has encouraged South Korean investment, is a two-term senator facing a competitive challenge from Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola.
Wednesday's Alaska event came two days after Mr. Trump announced plans for a $15 billion steel plant to be built in Iowa by a Minnesota company owned by an Indian industrial conglomerate.
In Iowa, Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson is in a close U.S. Senate contest with Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek for the seat being vacated by retiring two-term Republican Sen. Joni Ernst. Hinson spoke in the Oval Office during the announcement.
Alaska and Iowa — where Mr. Trump won comfortably each time he has run for president — are among the states where Democrats are targeting Republican-held Senate seats in the 2026 midterm elections, less than five weeks away.
Democrats need to gain a net of four seats in the 100-member Senate to overtake Republicans in the majority.

articles.title_orig: The Pentagon taps Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey to help decide what the military should do next
articles.title_zh: The Pentagon taps Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey to help decide what the military should do next
articles.content_orig:
The Pentagon is tapping Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk , defense technology entrepreneur and Anduril co-founder Palmer Luckey and former House Speaker Newt Gingrich to identify the military capabilities, technologies and weapons the U.S. may need in future wars, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Wednesday.
The initiative, dubbed Project Meridian, will spend 120 days looking years and decades ahead at how warfare could change and what capabilities the U.S. military will need to maintain a technological edge.
"Project Meridian, the future of warfare, is not about developing new strategies or new policies," Hegseth said. Instead, he said, its purpose is to "identify the domains that we must conquer, and capabilities we must master."
Hegseth said the effort will focus on “discovering, developing, and fielding” weapons and systems that future U.S. troops may need on battlefields ranging “from under the Earth to beyond the moon.” He announced the initiative during a "State of the Force" address to junior officers and enlisted leaders at Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia.
Pentagon technology chief Emil Michael will oversee the project, with Musk, Luckey and Gingrich as co-leads and a broader team drawn from government, industry, academia and the policy world, Hegseth said.
None of the three co-leads has served in the U.S. military. Musk moved to Canada as a teenager in part, he has said , to avoid compulsory military service in South Africa.
The role puts Musk and Luckey in prime position to help identify the military’s future technology needs while their companies compete for billions in DOD business.
Musk's SpaceX holds a plethora of Pentagon contracts. In May, the Space Force awarded the company a $4.16 billion contract to build satellites designed to track and target airborne threats, just days after awarding SpaceX another $2.29 billion contract for a military satellite communications network.
Luckey's Anduril develops autonomous weapons and other military technology. The Marine Corps awarded the company a contract worth up to $642 million in 2025 for counter-drone systems.
The announcement was part of a broader Pentagon push into autonomous warfare including plans announced Wednesday for a new four-star Autonomous Warfare Command aimed at scaling autonomous and robotic systems across the military.
Anduril, SpaceX, Tesla and Gingrich did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

articles.title_zh: Judge allows Paramount to close $110 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery
articles.content_orig:
A California judge on Wednesday formally approved Paramount Skydance’s settlement with California and other states, the final hurdle required for it to close its $110 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery.
Judge clears way for Paramount to acquire Warner Bros.
The seismic merger will bring together the likes of CBS News and CNN, HBO Max and Paramount+, and storied film studios Warner Bros. and Paramount Pictures.
Shortly after the judge’s approval, David Ellison, the CEO and controlling shareholder of Paramount Skydance, announced that Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz would become co-CEO of the combined media giant.
Kreiz will join the company Oct. 5, and the companies said in a statement the deal “is expected to close on October 6.”
“As Chairman & CEO, Ellison will lead all strategy, creative and technology while Kreiz, as Co-CEO will oversee the Company’s day-to-day operations and integration of the combined businesses,” the statement said.
Several outlets also reported this week that Paramount streaming chief Cindy Holland is departing the studio and Casey Bloys, HBO’s chief, will take on a new role running the combined streaming operations.
After the deal was approved by the U.S. Justice Department , the European Commission and dozens of other countries worldwide, it was held back by a lawsuit led by California’s Democratic attorney general, Rob Bonta.
Bonta and other state attorneys general worried that the deal, if completed, would reduce competition and potentially imperil the journalistic independence of CNN.
Paramount Skydance, led by Ellison, reached a deal with the states on Sept. 21 , which will require the combined company to release at least 30 films a year and set up an editorial board to oversee both CNN and CBS News.
Larry Ellison, the father of Paramount CEO David Ellison, is a close ally of President Donald Trump’s. He is personally backing the deal with tens of billions of dollars of his own fortune.
After acquiring Paramount, David Ellison appointed former New York Times opinion writer Bari Weiss to run CBS News. She has clashed with longtime correspondents and faced accusations of meddling with their editorial independence .
The merged company pledged to invest more than $1 billion in U.S. film production and worker training.
Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín’s approval comes just hours before a so-called ticking fee kicks in for Paramount Skydance.
In order to build confidence in the merger plan earlier this year, Paramount agreed to pay Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders 25 cents per share each quarter if the transaction did not close by Sept. 30. That penalty would be worth more than $600 million every three months.
“The parties reached their agreement following highly contested, however brief, litigation, and they reached their agreement following what they report to have been several rounds of in-depth negotiations,” Martínez-Olguín wrote in the order.
A spokesperson for the California Department of Justice said Wednesday that they are “pleased the court has approved our settlement.”
“Our settlement with Paramount resolves our antitrust concerns in every market we brought in our case, protects competition and consumer choice, and centers the needs, concerns, and futures of California workers,” the spokesperson said.
Some groups that opposed the merger, such as the Block the Merger coalition , urged in an amicus brief that the deal between the companies and states be rejected.
The group criticized the state attorneys general for what it called an “about-face” after suing to stop the deal. “The brief argues that small business owners and independent contractors will not receive the same handouts that members of major unions will if the consent decree is not upheld,” the group said.
“As for the so-called remedies the settlement offers, they do nothing to protect fair competition,” the group added.
Shares of both Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery closed near their highest levels of the day following the news. Paramount shares have been beaten down by more than 20% since the start of the year as the merger remained in limbo.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.
