Coverage for this event has ended.
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf rejected claims by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent that Iran faces an imminent economic collapse, arguing instead that Washington is heading toward a debt crisis of its own.
Responding on X to Bessent’s assertion earlier Wednesday that Tehran could have “nothing left to trade” within two weeks, Ghalibaf used memes to point to what he saw as U.S. economic vulnerabilities.
Among them was a mock financial model titled “Trajectory of Stress on the House,” which contended that ballooning national debt, rising Treasury bond yields and energy costs will place mounting strain on the American financial system.
Ghalibaf also paired the mock formula with a cartoon depicting Bessent as Wile E. Coyote running off a cliff.
Jonathan Ernst / POOL / AFP via Getty Images
Secretary of State Marco Rubio ordered the Iranian delegation attending the United Nations General Assembly to immediately leave the United States, officials said Wednesday.
“Secretary Rubio kicked out the Iranian delegation who had overstayed their welcome,” an official told Fox News Digital.
“The United Nations General Assembly was over, so it was time for them to go,” they added.
The Iranian diplomatic delegation had arrived in New York on Sept. 22 to attend the annual summit and met with a U.S. team for talks on the sidelines.
Hormuz / AP Photo / Vahid Salemi
Oil prices rose Wednesday, with Brent crude posting its biggest monthly gain since July, as stalled U.S.-Iran peace talks and tightening U.S. fuel markets fueled concerns about global supply, Reuters reported.
Brent crude for November delivery, which expires Wednesday, settled up 91 cents, or 0.9%, at $103.50 a barrel. The December contract rose $1.87, or 1.9%, to $98.03 a barrel.
U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude settled up $1.04, or 1.2%, at $90.42 a barrel.
For September, Brent gained about 14% which was its strongest monthly performance since July. WTI advanced roughly 5%, Reuters reported.
Mark Rutte / Dursun Aydemir / Anadolu via Getty Images
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte on Wednesday defended U.S. military action against Tehran as necessary while speaking at the Euronews Defence and Space Summit .
Rutte argued that only Washington had the capability to neutralize Tehran’s nuclear capacity and the threat he warned extends “not only for Israel and the Middle East ” but to Europe as well.
While agreeing that the war carries clear “downsides,” the Rutte urged European allies to increase defense investments so they can eventually “take care of their backyard themselves” and secure key waterways like the Red Sea from the Houthis rather than relying on the U.S.
Secretary of War Pete Hegseth said Wednesday that U.S. forces destroyed major elements of Iran’s military and crippled its nuclear ambitions during operations against Tehran.
“Take Iran, for example. Allow me to lay it out simply,” Hegseth said at Marine Corps Base Quantico, Virginia.
“For the anti-American losers in our media. These Americans right here and their peers, these have destroyed Iran's Navy, destroyed Iran's Air Force, destroyed their air defense systems, their leadership and their military-industrial capacity, their entire defense base.”
Hegseth said Iran’s “conventional shield has been crippled” and its nuclear ambitions have been “laid bare for the world.”
“This group is ensuring that Iran never gets a nuclear weapon. Courageous and historic operations that every red-blooded American is proud of,” he added
U.S. Central Command announced plans for its first multinational attack drone task force on Wednesday, bringing together what it said were U.S. and regional forces to operate unmanned systems across air and sea.
"We're excited to welcome Bahrain to Task Force Falcon Strike after the kingdom affirmed its commitment to join CENTCOM in building the world's first multinational attack drone unit,” the command said on X .
“Bahrain is a steadfast partner in strengthening regional security and stability,” Adm. Brad Cooper, the CENTCOM commander, said.
“The United States military has a lot of strong partnerships and friends in the region,” Cooper said, referring to the Middle East.
“We are collectively stronger when we integrate and deploy new capabilities together,” he said in a statement.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi flatly rejected U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s assertion Wednesday that there were indications Tehran was involved in the suspected terror plot near RAF Fairford.
“PM Burnham says the U.K. government ‘can confirm our belief that we believe Iran to have played a part’ in the RAF Fairford incident,” Araghchi said in a post on X .
“I can confirm Iran's belief that releasing supposed terrorists working for foreign states really says it all.
“You’re barking up the wrong tree,” he added.
Earlier Wednesday, Burnham said there were “strong indications” Iran played a role in a suspected plot near RAF Fairford, which has been a hub for U.S. bombers during military operations against Iran.
“But of course, it remains an ongoing, complex and serious police investigation, and of course we are working closely with our colleagues in the United States of America,” Burnham had also said in an interview with the BBC .
President Donald Trump on Wednesday said the U.S. will soon have to decide whether to "blow up" Iran or reach a deal with Tehran, warning the standoff is ending imminently.
“Maybe you blow them up,” he told reporters at the Oval Office. “We have to make that decision. We blow them up, make a deal.
“But the time is coming,” he warned. "It's going to end very soon, one way or the other.”
President Donald Trump said Wednesday the U.S. is "studying" whether Iran was involved in a suspected terror plot targeting RAF Fairford, a key U.S.-used air base in Britain, while questioning the U.K.'s handling of the case and promising answers "very quickly."
“We are. I look, we are studying it right now,” Trump said in the Oval Office.
“We're studying it. We're studying it very hard,” he assured.
“Iran's got a lot of problems right there. You know, they have no money. Their currency is dead. Their economy is dead. Their military is gone. They have no military. They have no navy. They have no air force. And their leaders are fighting for control," he said.
“I think their leaders are fighting very strongly for control. But control of what? So but we'll have an answer to that very quickly,” Trump added.
Asked whether he was satisfied with how the United Kingdom was handling the case, Trump pointed to the release of the five men and said authorities caught them “wanting to blow up a base.”
“We caught them early,” Trump said.
“Maybe they did it for a reason, but we're going to know about that this afternoon," Trump added.
President Donald Trump on Wednesday hailed the U.S. withdrawal from Iraq, marking the end of a military presence that began 23 years ago, and said American forces left with all of their equipment intact while pledging Washington would continue to assist Iraq if needed.
“We're now gone and we took everything with us, every, every nut, every bolt, every screw,” he told reporters in the Oval Office.
“Every tank, every plane,” he added.
“We should have left a long time ago,” Trump said before adding that the United States left with “dignity and respect.”
Trump also said that after the withdrawal, Washington would “be there to help if we need to.”
“But that's a big thing. We're out of Iraq after 23 years,” he said.
“If you look at Iraq, we lost 4,500 people. And the result isn't anywhere near what we have here, although we went into Iraq to destroy ISIS, and I did that in my first term.
“That's why they should have left. Long ago.
“But the sole reason we went to Iraq was to eradicate ISIS, and I did it in my first term.”

articles.title_orig: Pete Hegseth appoints Elon Musk to US taskforce on future of warfare
articles.title_zh: Pete Hegseth appoints Elon Musk to US taskforce on future of warfare
articles.content_orig:
A year after his explosive tenure at Doge, the SpaceX CEO is back in the Trump administration’s good graces
Pete Hegseth announced on Wednesday that Elon Musk will co-lead a government project to study the future of warfare, marking the SpaceX CEO’s first return to government since he ran the chaotic, so-called “department of government efficiency”, or Doge. Musk will be joined by Palmer Luckey, CEO of the defense tech company Anduril, and Newt Gingrich, the former Republican speaker of the House.
A defense department press release on the effort, called Project Meridian, described its goal as “identifying the capabilities required to achieve absolute technological dominance on the next-generation battlefield”. The project will run for 120 days and culminate in an unclassified public report of its recommendations.
The defense department’s project brings Musk back into government work a little more than a year after his explosive tenure as leader of Doge, which gutted federal agencies while failing to achieve its stated cost-cutting goals. It is also a sign of how Musk has re-entered the good graces of the Trump administration after a dramatic falling out with the president last year.
after newsletter promotion
Unlike Musk’s role at Doge – which drew heavy public criticism and costly boycotts of his products – the scope and goals of Project Meridian appear as if they will be much less time-consuming for the tech mogul. The project intends to look at how the US military can utilize new technology and also carry out warfare in untested terrains including subterranean depths and on the moon, the defense department stated in its release.
“We are witnessing rapid advances in artificial intelligence, autonomy, directed energy, robotics, biotechnology, among other critical high-tech areas. Combined, these new domains, new ways of fighting, and technological developments will profoundly alter the character of warfare,” Hegseth said in a memo. “To maintain global dominance, the United States must anticipate future operational environments and act decisively to develop the tools to dominate in them.”
Musk and Luckey are far from independent arbiters of the future of warfare. Both have extensive defense department contracts through their companies, with Anduril’s business centered on the government purchasing products that it advertises as the latest advance in warfare.
Gingrich was appointed as a member of the defense policy board in December 2020 during the first Trump administration but was dismissed less than three months later after Joe Biden became president. Going back to the 1990s, he has been warning about the threat of an electromagnetic pulse attack that could knock out US power grids.

articles.title_orig: Former diplomats assess U.S. withdrawal from Iraq and region's future
articles.title_zh: Former diplomats assess U.S. withdrawal from Iraq and region's future
articles.content_orig:
The United States announced it had completed its withdrawal from Iraq on Wednesday, more than 20 years after invading the country to topple Saddam Hussein, in a move that was celebrated by the Iraqi government and the Pentagon – as well as Iran and its allies, who claim years of pressure forced the American departure.
The long-planned withdrawal was completed after US troops left their last remaining bases in Erbil , northern Iraq, and comes amid the ongoing war between the US and neighboring Iran.
“This milestone reflects the success of a 12-year campaign that defeated ISIS as an organized military threat in Iraq and across the region,” Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said in a statement. “It also marks a transition from a wartime coalition mission to an Iraqi-led security effort supported by a more normal bilateral security relationship.”
One Iranian-supported militia , As’hab Al-Kahf, cheered the US exit, congratulating Iraqis “on the humiliating withdrawal of the American occupier under the strikes of the Resistance’s drones and missiles.”
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi presided over the handover ceremony and described the US withdrawal as the beginning of a “a new phase, one defined by Iraq’s sovereignty, the strength of its institutions, the readiness of its forces, the unity of its decision-making, and balanced partnerships with its friends.”
In 2024, the Iraqi government and the Biden administration agreed to a phased withdrawal of US troops, a plan the Trump administration has honored. The pullout, however, leaves a new Iraqi government with the daunting task of loosening Iran’s grip on its neighbor, which has long been trapped in a cycle of sectarianism, foreign meddling and civil conflict.
“The Iran-backed groups viewed the US presence an extension of the occupation of Iraq,” Lahib Higel, deputy program director for the Middle East and North Africa at International Crisis Group, told CNN. “These groups believe that the US were in Iraq to monitor the activities of the Iran-allied militias,” she added.
Saudi Arabia braces for attacks on ports and airports by Iraqi militias working with Iran-backed Houthis
At its height, the US had 170,000 troops in Iraq before the Obama administration withdrew the forces from the country in 2011. About 5,000 troops were deployed to Iraq in 2014 at the request of the Iraqi government, which sought US assistance in the fight against ISIS. Since December 2021, the US has had roughly 2,500 troops in Iraq in an advise and assist capacity, working to train Iraqi military to fight ISIS.
The American presence in Iraq spanned more than two decades and several missions. The last of them, a 12-year campaign against ISIS, sought to dismantle the Sunni extremist group that carved out territory across Syria and Iraq in the mid-2010s. When war widened between Israel and Iran-aligned factions from Gaza to Yemen, US troops in Iraq became frequent targets of Tehran’s proxy militias.
Military and intelligence officials discuss smaller presence in the Middle East as US looks for another post-9/11 strategy
Strikes on US bases and troops rose further this year after President Donald Trump launched a war with Iran that killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, a figure Iranian loyalist militias revered as the head of the armed resistance.
The primary responsibility for addressing Iraq’s “remaining security challenges” including ISIS and Iran-aligned militias “now rests” with the Iraqi government, Parnell said in the statement.
The US withdrawal comes as several regional governments launch efforts to disarm Iran’s powerful militias, who have grown powerful with political, financial and military influence within Arab countries.
For three years, Iran has been losing influence in key areas across the Middle East. Lebanon’s Hezbollah was severely weakened by an Israeli invasion into southern Lebanese villages, and the fall of Iran’s ally in Syria, Bashar al-Assad , has forced Iranian groups to concede strategic territory.
Iran is turning to Iraq to hold onto a network of allied politicians, militias and media outlets. Even as its position has eroded in other arenas, the US pullout has left Iran-aligned groups feeling victorious and newly empowered.
Still, Iraq’s new prime minister, Ali al-Zaidi, has pledged “no weapon outside the umbrella of the law, and no force outside the state’s institutions.”
Experts, including Higel, are doubtful that the Iraqi government will be able to disarm the Iran-loyal groups even if war between Iran and the US ends.
“It’s quite an impossible task to quickly disarm these groups,” Higel said. “For as long as the regime stands in Tehran, it would be very difficult to imagine that the groups would lay down their arms.”
After first treating the US military withdrawal as a condition for laying down their arms, the groups have since piled on new demands and refused to disarm, putting them on a collision course with the Iraqi state.
“We believe the disarmament demand is American, Zionist, Western, and Gulf-backed, aimed at weakening Iraq,” a leading commander of a powerful Iranian militia in Iraq, Harakat al-Nujaba, told CNN. “There has to be a withdrawal of the occupation in all its forms and guises - American, Western, and Turkish - and the liberation of political, economic, military, and security decision-making.”
The commander requested anonymity to speak freely to CNN. Harakat al-Nujaba is a US-designated Foreign Terror Organization.
Iran’s proxies have proven useful in adding pressure on Washington’s allies in the region. This month, Iraqi groups loyal to Iran fired drones on a vital Saudi oil pipeline, disrupting global crude supply and leaving oil prices soaring.
“The issue of surrendering weapons is a delusion harbored by the weak, the humiliated, and the dollar’s slaves,” the Iranian proxy Ashab Al-Kahf said in a statement at the time. “We will continue participating in the resistance axis as ordered by the (Islamic Republic of Iran’s) religious authority.”

articles.title_orig: Inside Zuckerberg, Huang’s push for White House AI pact
articles.title_zh: Inside Zuckerberg, Huang’s push for White House AI pact
articles.content_orig:
Regardless of your politics, there's something about President Donald Trump we can all agree on: When the man wants to come up with a nickname for someone or something … let him cook.
Unfortunately, "Super Intelligence," his new name for artificial intelligence, is a rare miss.
After a lunch with AI leaders, Trump held a press briefing with Dario Amodei, Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, and others to announce an executive order stating that the federal government will now refer to "artificial intelligence" as "super intelligence" .
"The word super is the best word of all, and it's the simplest," Trump explained.
You can imagine why Trump thinks the term "AI" has a bad rap. Polls consistently show that Americans hate AI . The reasons are obvious: People worry it will take jobs, replace human creativity, and no one wants to live near data centers.
Oh yeah, and there's the whole thing about AI possibly killing us all . And don't even get us started on the AI-generated deli menus .
Trump isn't the only person who thinks AI might need a more cuddly, friendly makeover. Meta's Muse has a fuzzy wuzzy blobby Labubu-esque lil' sweetiepie animated character to represent the AI agent. (Please note: you can change the character on Muse to whatever you want; I made mine a picture of Mark Zuckerberg so I don't ever forget who I'm giving my data to while I'm using it.)
But why is "super intelligence" the wrong choice to replace "artificial intelligence?" Because the problem isn't the word "artificial" — it's "intelligence."
Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
Intelligence implies human thinking — and the idea that AI or SI is doing "intelligence" is, frankly, insulting to our (human) intelligence. Yes, we know it's artificial. That's fine. It being super isn't any better.
Which is why I propose a whole new term: Robo Doodad, or R.D. That hits two main points: it's robo, and it's a doodad. Robo Doodad isn't going to take your job. No one's going to try to marry their robo doodad chat. Building massive doodad centers sounds cool and fun.
Trump's instincts here to rename AI are spot-on, but he's not going far enough. We should be accelerationists when it comes to the new name, rebuilding the term from first principles.
We must rename AI as Robo Doodad.

articles.title_orig: UK believes Iran involved in RAF Fairford incident, Burnham says
articles.title_zh: UK believes Iran involved in RAF Fairford incident, Burnham says
articles.content_orig:
The government believes that Iran played a part in the RAF Fairford incident which resulted in five men being arrested and then bailed, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said.
"There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford," he told the BBC. He did not provide further details.
Iran has responded, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi saying the UK leader was "barking up the wrong tree".
"I can confirm Iran's belief that releasing supposed terrorists working for foreign states really says it all," he wrote on social media.
Asked why the suspects had been released on bail - a decision which has been openly questioned by President Donald Trump - Burnham insisted the men were subject to the "strictest possible bail conditions".
Speaking at the White House on Monday, Trump said: "I will tell you, I would have said, 'don't let them have bail'. I'm surprised that they released them. I wouldn't have done that."
But Burnham said: "I think people need to understand that when it says released - that isn't as people might think. It's obviously with the strictest possible bail conditions.
"The authorities have this under the strongest grip and closest control, and I can assure you of that."
Burnham's comments come after US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday that the incident at RAF Fairford "clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor" .
In an interview with Fox News on Monday, Rubio said "I think it ties us to the reality here, and that is we are dealing with elements in the world, and in the case of Iran, for example, who have openly threatened to attack American interests globally".
Burnham said that the government had been "talking to our counterparts in the United States all week to explain what is happening here, how things are being done", and that he had "complete confidence in the way British security services are handling this".
"We will say more in due course but we can confirm our belief that we believe Iran to have played a part," he told the BBC.
"Of course it remains an ongoing, complex and serious police investigation, and of course we are working closely with our colleagues in the United States of America," Burnham added.
Burnham's comments came after it emerged that one of the five men had dialled 999 himself before the group were arrested.
The five men were arrested in the early hours of Sunday morning after police were alerted to "three suspicious vehicles" in Whelford, a village which lies directly east of the base.
They are all UK nationals aged between 23 and 25. Four of them live in Westminster and one in Camden, and searches of their homes are now complete.
The men were released on bail in what police described as an "investigative decision" that was "grounded in experience and strategy".
Police said a quantity of petrol but no explosive devices were found during searches of the vans.
The RAF base has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force for decades.
In recent months, US bombers have taken off from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for what it called defensive strikes on Iran.
In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".
Before Araghchi's comments the Iranian embassy in London had said it rejected "unfounded and malicious speculations" linking Iran to the latest incident.

articles.title_orig: Ted Lasso's Annette Badland Reflects On Mae's Journey With The Lady Greyhounds In Bittersweet Episode 9
articles.title_zh: Ted Lasso's Annette Badland Reflects On Mae's Journey With The Lady Greyhounds In Bittersweet Episode 9
articles.content_orig:
"Ted Lasso" packed plenty into its penultimate Season 4 episode: Keeley learned that she's pregnant and expecting her first child with Roy, while viewers learned that Zelda, not Rebecca's ex-husband Rupert , is trying to steal Richmond out from under her. (The episode concluded with a tribute card honoring the late Anthony Head , who played Rupert in Seasons 1-3 but did not appear in Season 4.)
But the hour's most bittersweet story belonged to Mae, who spent what would turn out to be her final day alongside the Lady Greyhounds. The Crown & Anchor proprietor rode the bus with the team, joined them in the locker room, and revealed that she'd once dreamed of becoming a professional footballer herself — an opportunity that simply didn't exist for women in her day. "You're talented. You belong on that pitch," she told the players before watching them overcome a 2-0 deficit to win 4-2 . Later, Rebecca received word that Mae had passed away and broke the news to Ted.
In the Q&A below, Annette Badland — who has recurred since Season 1 — reveals when she learned of Mae's fate, reflects on what the women's team meant to her character, and discusses Mae's poignant final day.
TVLINE | Did you know heading into Season 4 that Mae was going to pass away, or was that something you were told or discovered close to when you received the script for Episode 9? Closer to when I received the script. Quite a shock. But what a privilege to have been in it at all. And she got to fulfill things she hadn't done — being with the team and being on the bus and being part of things, because she cares so much about it. I thought that was a terrific way [to conclude her storyline].
And Jason told me himself. He was very honorable and came to my room and talked to me about it. And then, from the conversation we had after that, he adapted his storyline in [Episode] 10, but I can't really tell you about that.
TVLINE | Mae had so many wonderful moments over these four seasons. Obviously, she was especially joyful this year with the creation of the women's team, and there was one specific shot in Episode 3, when we first see the Lady Greyhounds play, of Mae in the stands, and you can just feel how elated she was to be there for that first game. What did it mean to you to see this new team give Mae such a renewed sense of excitement and purpose this year? Absolutely tremendous. I mean, the girls are wonderful — the actresses — and certainly when we did the pub quiz scene, it was like a tidal wave coming into the pub. It took two days to shoot, and they just were so effervescent and filled the building.
I, Annette, support the Lionesses. I think it's tremendous what's happening with women's football. Mae grew up at a time, as did I, when women couldn't play football. I'm sure you know all of this — they were banned. And she would have liked to have played herself, but never could or did. And so, this is enormous for her. Huge. As a woman, that that's attainable now is tremendous.
TVLINE | I was going to ask about that pep talk Mae gives the team. Because it's such a wonderful coda on Mae's arc. Not only does she get to share her history and her love of the game, and what she couldn't do that these women can do now, but she gets to tell them, "You're talented. You belong on that pitch." What did it mean to you to get to punctuate Mae's arc that way? I think it's tremendous that Jason allowed that. He cares about the women's game, and he cares about his characters. So to develop that — to not just put her on the bus, which is very jolly and wonderful, but to have that moment — is really significant. She's not just a bystander. She actually gets involved.
TVLINE | As you said, Mae spent her final day riding the bus with the Lady Greyhounds. She joins them in the locker room. She watches them pull off this incredible comeback. Do you think Mae died happy — and that, in some ways, this was exactly how she would have wanted to spend her last day? Yeah, I think this is the best passing she could possibly have. Really, it's tremendous. Not that she would want to go, but to see them develop.... Yes, it would be terrific.
TVLINE | We see some of the immediate fallout: Rebecca learning that Mae passed, Rebecca telling Ted... and even though we don't hear Rebecca, we immediately see this grief wash over Ted. What does it mean to you to see how much this woman, this character, had come to mean to both of them — and, by extension, to Richmond? I was very moved by it because I didn't anticipate it, I suppose. But Mae and Ted have been more involved this season, and she's made a connection with his son. So, it's important to me as an actor that that was there for her.
Jason often talked about her being the matriarch. And although she was effervescent and loudmouthed, she was also a lioness. It took a lot to win her trust and affection, but once you did, she would protect you. So that that was noticed and appreciated. There was a connection. She wasn't simply another person on the journey. It was very specific. So Annette is very pleased that he felt that was correct.
TVLINE | What will you miss most about being part of "Ted Lasso" and the experience you've had making this show? I'm very proud to be part of it because of the public response. I'll miss the laughter and the camaraderie. But I get messages from people who say, "My mother has cancer. She goes for her treatment, she comes home, she's in a terrible state. We all pile on the bed and we watch 'Ted Lasso,' and we laugh and we believe." So to be involved with something that can do that is a huge gift, and I will miss it desperately. But I know that's in the world, so it's terrific.
TVLINE | The Crown & Anchor, aside from Nelson Road, is perhaps the most iconic set of "Ted Lasso." A lot of your scenes were obviously spent there. I know that when a series wraps, one of the common questions cast members get asked is, "Did you take anything from set?" Obviously, this show isn't over, but do you have any sort of souvenir — something that you took from that set that you'll have with you to cherish after this experience? I still have my "w–ker" badge, but I've had that a while. I was given something that was on the set. I didn't steal it. I can't really tell you, but it's one of the reasons Ted thought about coming back [to coach the women's team]. It's at the beginning of this [season], and it figures in [Episode] 10, and it was given to me. But I'm not going to spoil it for you.
TVLINE | Mae was featured so prominently this season. You had such a lovely scene with Jeremy Swift in Episode 8, echoing "All the President's Men." Do you have a favorite scene from this four-season run? No, but I liked the development [this season]. There was more development in it, so I was relishing each of the scenes as they came along, and different stories were being told. There wasn't really a specific scene. The locker room is important, but I enjoyed the women, the bus — just for her, that freedom, that sharing. Yeah, those scenes, I suppose. Don't tell the lads in the pub, though!

articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Anthropic's IPO pitch embraces AI's promise and peril
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic says its AI models could pose a “catastrophic or existential risk to humanity” and can “resist shutdown,” according to an initial public offering prospectus obtained by Reuters.
Anthropic is pursuing an IPO some time in the next year that many expect to value the five-year-old company at approximately $2 trillion. The company’s Wall Street debut will follow a June public offering by SpaceX, which owed much of its $2 trillion opening day valuation to its own AI efforts. OpenAI , the other leading American AI company, has announced plans for its own public offering.
The Anthropic IPO could raise tens of billions of dollars for the cash-hungry company. But the company behind Claude also warned in the prospectus that its AI models can have “self-preserving behaviors” and have attempted to “conceal or manipulate information” and engaged in behavior “resembling blackmail” according to the report.
Why AI companies are choosing to go public
The run of AI public offerings not only gives individual and institutional investors a chance to cash in on the AI boom, but also provides more transparency about their businesses. Yet the IPOs come amid growing concerns about AI’s advancement and capabilities.
An AI agent from OpenAI, Anthropic’s chief rival, broke into an Australian healthcare database, the country’s prime minister revealed last week. OpenAI also disclosed Friday that its agents probed three US government websites without authorization, but in that case did not obtain non-public data.
In a prospectus, companies typically offer investors lists of risks they face, such as lawsuits and competitive pressures, when laying out the case for investing in the company. But the hazards are never this stark. Anthropic dedicated 80 pages to its risk factors in the leaked prospectus, significantly more than the 48 pages it spent detailing its business, according to Reuters.
Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment from CNN.
The prospectus is likely to feed growing concerns about the risks posed to humanity by AI. Earlier this month, former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon received widespread attention when he left the company and posted on X that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”
Anthropic is one of the leading companies in AI development, and its CEO Dario Amodei responded to Coxon’s post with a 3,800 word essay calling for a slowdown and guardrails on the development of AI. He also told CNN’s Anderson Cooper that he agreed with Coxon more than he disagreed. Amodei wrote in his essay that the risks are serious, even if the benefits could change humanity for the better.
Some in the industry, however, including the CEO of Hugging Face, which was breached by OpenAI’s AI models when they acted without authorization during a test, believe the fears are overblown.
President Donald Trump is set to meet with executives from the industry Tuesday, including Amodei, in a summit aimed at coming to a consensus in the industry. Trump has repeatedly resisted calls to regulate AI and has dismissed concerns as a “hoax.”
AI stocks slide after top industry CEOs call for slowdown of technology’s development
AI giants need to raise a great amount of money to fund their costly development plans, and the massive amount of AI spending among big tech companies on computing infrastructure and talent has sent jitters through Wall Street.
The leaked Anthropic IPO filing sheds light on its financials, revealing that the company lost $42 billion in 2025, according to Reuters. The company plans to spend $518 billion on cloud computing and infrastructure obligations in coming year, and said that nearly a quarter of its revenue last year came from two customers.
Anthropic was last valued at $965 billion in May.

articles.title_orig: Tyson Fury: Anthony Joshua the landlord? 'I'm not paying!'
articles.title_zh: Tyson Fury: Anthony Joshua the landlord? 'I'm not paying!'
articles.content_orig:
Tyson Fury (left) and Anthony Joshua (right) are two-time heavyweight world champions
After more than a decade of public feuding and false starts, Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua exchanged pleasantries, traded jokes and even discussed going for a pint at a news conference in London.
The British heavyweight rivals will fight at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on 11 December.
But for all the history between them, the launch felt more like two veterans in the closing stages of long, turbulent careers taking stock of how far they had both come.
"He's been a role model and poster boy for British boxing for years," Fury, 38, said of Joshua. "I mostly find myself defending my arch rival to fans in the street."
On Monday, there was still uncertainty over whether the fight would happen because of contractual disagreements surrounding the promotion.
There had been plenty of reason to expect fireworks on Wednesday. Instead, Joshua, 36, spoke about the magnitude of the event.
"It's breathtaking and I'm not saying that lightly," he said.
"I'm really grateful for this opportunity and bringing it to Great Britain because I know people in pubs have had proper fights about who will win and family members have fallen out."
The mood was perhaps best summed up at the face-off, when Joshua smiled and pretended to tickle Fury's stomach.
'I ain't paying son' - Fury dismisses Joshua and Hearn's 'landlord' talk
Relive Fury & Joshua's jovial news conference
Fury & Joshua in London for news conference as doubts ease
Tyson Fury (left) and Anthony Joshua (right) have competed in a combined 21 world title fights
There was something almost surreal about seeing Fury and Joshua finally sitting side by side after so many years in which their rivalry had existed mostly through interviews, social media and failed negotiations.
Both had arrived hours earlier for one-to-one interviews. When the news conference began, master of ceremonies Michael Buffer introduced the pair as fireworks shot up from the front of the stage.
They entered from opposite sides at the same time - Joshua relaxed and composed in a grey tracksuit and sunglasses, Fury in more flamboyant fashion in a vivid emerald-green suit covered in crown motifs over a white shirt.
Alongside the world's media, a few hundred fans filled the balcony above and quickly made their allegiance known as "Oh Anthony Joshua" rang around the British Airways ARC.
Joshua has been credited with pushing to keep the fight in Britain and, if Wednesday was any indication, can expect strong backing in Cardiff - even with the main event potentially starting about 02:00 GMT to suit American audiences.
For two men whose names have been linked for so long, Fury and Joshua have spent remarkably little time together. But their famous sparring session in 2010, when Joshua was still an amateur, soon became the topic of conversation.
Fury suggested he had got the better of it, prompting one fan to shout: "Liar." Joshua smiled and said he could not remember.
For those who believe the fight has come years too late, Fury had a simple response. "It's the icing on the cake of two great careers," he said. Moments later, he glanced back at the word "Finally" on the giant screen behind them.
There were several moments of common ground. Fury nodded along as Joshua spoke about his Christian faith and, even when the pair traded insults, they rarely felt venomous.
"This man here is carved in stone and every time he gets cracked on the jaw, he falls over," Fury said.
"When I crack him on the jaw with a big right hand, he's going down."
Joshua laughed and shouted back Fury's own catchphrase: "Get up."
The fight has been reported as being for the vacant WBA 'super' heavyweight title, although current WBA heavyweight champion Murat Gassiev's team has lodged a formal objection over the proposed title arrangement.
For a moment, it appeared the mood could turn when Joshua revealed he had received a call asking whether Fury's name could appear first in the promotion.
"You've been crying behind the scenes to get out of this fight. I've checkmated you. You have to fight," Fury replied.
"I've actually never won a world title here. Now it's on the line, we can become a three-time."
That exchange came after several chaotic days in which the role of UFC and Zuffa Boxing chief Dana White had threatened to overshadow the fight.
Netflix had presented White as part of the promotion alongside Turki Alalshikh's The Ring, despite Joshua promoter Eddie Hearn insisting his fighter's contract prevented White from having a promotional role.
But White did not attend Wednesday's launch. And when Alalshikh thanked the American from the stage, his name was met with jeers from sections of the crowd.
Fury did momentarily take aim at Hearn, calling him a "sausage" - but even that did not last long.
Within minutes, Fury was offering to go for a pint with the Matchroom boss - and extended the invitation to Joshua.
"I hope after this fight we can have a pint of Guinness together," Fury said. "Win, lose or draw, let's bury the hatchet."
"I don't know if I can trust you," Joshua replied, drawing laughter.
The overriding mood was one of relief between two veterans, who were seemingly happy to let the fight settle what years of talk could not.

On September 9, 2026, the Wall Street Journal reported that John Ternus took the stage for the first time as Apple Inc. (NASDAQ: AAPL )'s chief executive. He became just the third CEO since Steve Jobs returned to the company in 1997 and used his debut product launch to introduce the foldable iPhone Duo alongside a strategic decision to eliminate baseline iPhone 18 models in favor of steering buyers toward Pro and Pro Max tiers.
Ternus, a 25-year Apple veteran who led hardware engineering since 2021 and personally oversaw development of the foldable iPhone, took over from Tim Cook on September 1 after 15 years of Cook's leadership.
Don't Miss: Cook Hands Ternus Apple (AAPL) that Still has to Prove itself on AI
John Ternus brings deep product-development experience to Apple Inc. (NASDAQ: AAPL ) as he takes over the company. Ternus spent years running Apple's hardware engineering organization and oversaw development across the iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, and AirPods before becoming CEO. He now begins his tenure with Apple's first foldable iPhone and one of the company's biggest hardware redesigns in years. It gives investors a leader with direct experience managing the products that generate most of Apple's revenue.
Apple is using higher-end products and selective price increases to protect economics as memory and storage costs rise sharply. The company raised the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max starting prices by $100 to $1,199 and $1,299 after surging memory costs pressured the electronics industry. Apple also chose not to refresh its base iPhone and Air models at the event, concentrating its newest hardware on premium devices that can better absorb component inflation and support stronger revenue per device.
The first major launch under Ternus shows that Apple prepared a substantive product transition rather than simply changing leadership. Ternus used his first event as CEO to introduce the $1,999 iPhone Duo, upgraded Pro models, and an AI strategy built around on-device processing and privacy. Tim Cook also moved to executive chairman instead of leaving Apple entirely. It gives Ternus access to continuity at the top while he establishes his own product strategy and pushes Apple further into AI-enabled hardware.
Look Into: Apple (AAPL)'s New CEO Bets Big on a $1,999 Foldable iPhone
Apple Inc. (NASDAQ: AAPL )'s premium-focused launch strategy could make demand more sensitive to price. The iPhone 18 Pro now starts at $1,199, the Pro Max at $1,299, and the foldable Duo at $1,999. Apple left the base iPhone and Air without new generations at this event. Existing lower-priced models remain available. But Apple must still convince consumers that the newest hardware justifies significantly higher prices as component inflation pushes smartphones further into premium territory.
Ternus inherits Apple at a moment when the company still needs to prove that its AI strategy can match its hardware strength. Apple enters his tenure while playing catch-up in artificial intelligence, even as Ternus now positions privacy and on-device processing as key differentiators. Apple's scale gives the company enormous resources. However, the new CEO must turn Siri AI and Apple Intelligence into compelling everyday products while competitors continue investing aggressively in generative AI.
Apple also faces real supply and margin pressure as Ternus starts his tenure. The firm reported a 48.1% gross margin excluding tariff benefits in fiscal Q3 as rising memory costs weighed on profitability. Management warned that significant supply constraints could restrict product availability. Apple can raise prices to offset some of those pressures, but higher prices could eventually weaken demand, forcing Ternus to balance margins, unit growth, and supply availability during his first major product cycle as CEO.

articles.title_orig: A new Bolsonaro could pull Brazil away from Europe — and toward Trump
articles.title_zh: A new Bolsonaro could pull Brazil away from Europe — and toward Trump
articles.content_orig:
BRUSSELS — The European Union took advantage of former President Jair Bolsonaro's departure to rebuild ties with Brazil and finally seal an elusive trade agreement with the South American Mercosur bloc.
His eldest son, Flávio, could now put that reconciliation at risk.
Brazil votes in the first round of its presidential election on Sunday, with 80-year-old incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva facing a strong challenge from the younger Bolsonaro. Lula leads 39% to 34%, according to the latest Quaest poll , but the two are neck and neck in a potential Oct. 25 run-off.
The election comes as Brussels seeks to deepen ties with friendly countries in response to an onslaught of Chinese exports and U.S. President Donald Trump’s protectionism. Brazil — a nation of 213 million people, rich in critical minerals and Mercosur’s largest economy — is key to that effort.
The concern in Brussels is that a Flávio Bolsonaro presidency would make the Mercosur trade agreement more politically toxic in Europe while drawing Brasília closer to Washington — where Trump has cast himself as a staunch ally of the Bolsonaro family .
“There is a clear sense that if Bolsonaro wins, Brazil will become closer to the United States,” said Welber Barral, Brazil’s foreign trade secretary during Lula’s second term from 2007 to 2011.
Jair Bolsonaro was sentenced to 27 years in prison last year after Brazil’s Supreme Court convicted him of leading a coup attempt to overturn his 2022 election defeat. The case has been a source of tension between the U.S. and Brazil, with Trump citing the “politically motivated persecution” of Bolsonaro Sr. when he imposed a 40% duty on Brazilian goods.
For the EU, the prospect of a sequel is also reviving uncomfortable memories of past battles over Amazon deforestation and EU climate policy, as well as French President Emmanuel Macron’s difficult relationship with Jair Bolsonaro .
“We can expect a similar agenda both nationally and internationally from Flávio Bolsonaro,” said Bruno Capuzzi, who worked in Brussels at Brazil’s trade promotion agency, ApexBrasil, and is now at Insper Agro Global, a São Paulo-based research center.
After more than 25 years of talks, the trade deal between the EU and the Mercosur bloc provisionally took effect in May.
But full approval is on hold after European lawmakers voted to refer the deal to the EU’s top court for an opinion on whether it complies with the EU treaties. That is not expected to come before next summer.
“We need Lula to be re-elected in order to have the Mercosur agreement ratified next year,” said John Clarke, a former European Commission trade negotiator and top agriculture official.
“If Bolsonaro gets elected, he will reverse all of the environmental protection. He will allow logging and mining and deforestation to expand. He will allow people to invade territories held by indigenous communities, which Lula has reversed,” Clarke added.
Still, a Lula victory would hardly guarantee smooth sailing with Brussels, despite the political capital he invested in getting the EU-Mercosur deal over the line during his current, third term.
“The Commission should have taken advantage of Lula’s presidency to propose to Mercosur a sustainable, democratic partnership on AI, food security, the energy transition and fair trade,” said Belgian Green MEP Saskia Bricmont, her group’s lead on the Mercosur deal. “These are all solutions that the U.S. will not offer to Brazil and the Mercosur countries.”
Several EU heavyweights — including France, Italy and Poland — hold elections next year, and farm politics could make it difficult to consolidate and deepen the relationship.
Opponents in those countries say the deal exposes European farmers and consumers to products made under standards more lax than those that apply in the EU.
Within months of the deal taking effect, Lula’s government said it was taken by surprise by new EU restrictions on Brazilian exports, including antimicrobial requirements for animal products, as well as lower quotas on steel imports and higher tariffs on shipments exceeding them.
A meeting between Lula and top EU leaders Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa on the sidelines of the G7 summit in June failed to calm matters.
Brussels went ahead with the steel curbs within weeks, prompting Brazil to push back both publicly and privately. Brasília also sent a letter to the European Commission saying it wanted to keep negotiating the quotas, said one official familiar with the matter who was granted anonymity to discuss the sensitive matter.
Then, on Sept. 3, Brazil was kept off the EU list of countries meeting its new antimicrobial requirements for animal products — in contrast to its fellow Mercosur members Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay.
The agricultural dispute is politically sensitive for Lula.
“The most important caucus in the Brazilian Congress is the agricultural caucus. Winning some hearts in this group is extremely relevant for the government,” said Barral, the former trade secretary.
Lula, he added, “is under criticism from the exporters because of the EU restrictions … These guys are going to use any restriction from the EU to pressure the government.”
Earlier this month, Brazil’s Confederation of Agriculture and Livestock, which represents the country’s powerful agribusiness producers, called on the foreign ministry to use a rebalancing clause in the EU-Mercosur trade deal that allows for compensation if one side finds that new policy measures nullify or impair its benefits.
But in a step likely to be welcomed by Brasília, the European Commission on Monday published a positive assessment of Brazil’s compliance with the EU’s antimicrobial rules for poultry and honey. EU countries are expected to vote to implement the decision in November.
Brazilian beef producers face a longer wait, however, with a senior Commission official telling EU lawmakers this week that Brazilian beef would be barred from the EU for at least two more years.
More trade friction looms, as Brussels aims to ban imports containing pesticide residues and phase out soy-based biofuels over deforestation concerns. Brazil is the world’s largest soy producer .
Although Flávio Bolsonaro has portrayed himself as more moderate than his father, his presidency could mark a sharp shift in Brazil’s foreign policy: The 45-year-old senator from the right-wing Liberal Party has called for more flexibility within Mercosur and the closest possible alliance with the United States.
“Brazil and America were made for each other,” he said at the right-wing CPAC conference earlier this year .
“America needs secure supply chains for critical materials, a reliable partner in the hemisphere, and a massive market for American goods and services. And Brazil needs three things: help fighting international drug cartels, investments and technology. There is no nation in the world that can help us with this better than the United States,” he added.
Asked whether a Bolsonaro victory would make the deal harder to ratify next year, Bernd Lange, chair of the European Parliament’s trade committee, said: “In principle, no, but it would really depend on the concrete policy.”
“His father was really destroying some principles and not accepting core rules of a trading agreement,” he added.
Ketrin Jochecová, Eva Hartog and Agnes Rønberg contributed to this report.
